title: The Next Four Years Will Decide the Ocean’s Future
content:
This summer, the ocean sent us another warning. In August, global sea-surface temperatures reached their highest level on record. Days later, the most comprehensive assessment of coral reefs ever published showed that increasingly frequent marine heatwaves are leaving reefs less time to recover between bleaching events. Global hard coral cover has declined by 9.5% compared with the 1980-2009 average, driven primarily by human-induced climate change.
For me, this is deeply concerning, but also a reason to act. I come from Seychelles, an archipelago of 115 islands off the coast of East Africa where the ocean is inseparable from our lives, livelihoods, and future. It supports the food we eat, the jobs people depend on, and the resilience of our economy.
During my years in office, I saw what is possible when governments make ocean protection a political priority. In 2020, during my presidency, Seychelles designated 30% of its waters for protection, years before the world adopted the global goal of protecting 30% of land and ocean by 2030. That experience taught me that ambitious conservation is possible when political commitment is matched by action.
With fewer than four years remaining until 2030, the international community needs to bring that same determination to protecting the global ocean.
Since governments adopted the global goal in 2022, countries have made important progress. Nearly 20% of land and inland waters are now designated as protected or conserved, and existing commitments could bring terrestrial protection to around 27% by 2030.
But the picture at sea is very different. Around 10% of the global ocean is currently designated as protected or conserved, and existing commitments would raise that figure to only around 12% by 2030.
The next phase of this global effort must therefore put much greater emphasis on the ocean. Governments need to establish more marine protected areas, strengthen national commitments where ambition remains too low, and move rapidly from targets to protection in the water.
This matters far beyond conservation. Healthy marine ecosystems support fisheries and food security, sustain livelihoods and economies, store carbon, and help protect coastal communities from climate impacts.
The recent coral findings make the consequences of delay clear. Marine heatwaves are becoming more frequent, leaving reefs less time to recover. Recovery is still possible, but ecosystems need time and the right conditions to recover.
Climate action remains essential, but reducing pressures such as overfishing, pollution and damaging extraction can give vulnerable ecosystems a better chance of recovery. Well-designed and properly managed marine protected areas can give nature the space and time it needs.
But drawing a boundary on a map is not enough. The 2026 Ocean Protection Gap Report finds that while around 10% of the global ocean is designated as protected or conserved, just 3.5% is assessed as effectively protected. A protected area cannot fulfill its purpose if damaging activities continue, management is weak, or long-term finance is missing.
In Seychelles, we are confronting this challenge ourselves. Having designated more than 30% of our waters for protection, we are now undertaking the harder work of turning those protections into results in the water. Our Marine Spatial Plan Initiative is legally binding, including no-take areas where extractive activities are prohibited. But effective protection also requires management, monitoring, enforcement and long-term resources.
The next four years, through the end of 2030, must therefore be about both expansion and effectiveness. Success should be judged by area on a map, and by whether biodiversity recovers and communities continue to benefit from healthy ecosystems.
National action alone cannot close the ocean protection gap. The high seas account for roughly two-thirds of the global ocean, yet only a very small share is protected. Species migrate across borders, currents connect ecosystems, and damage in one part of the ocean can have consequences far beyond it.
The High Seas Treaty changes what is possible. For the first time, governments have a global legal framework capable of enabling marine protected areas beyond national jurisdiction. Seychelles became the first African country to ratify the treaty because island states understand that protecting our own waters is not enough. Our future also depends on the ocean we share.
Governments now need to turn this legal breakthrough into protection in the water by advancing an ambitious first generation of high seas marine protected areas, supported by strong science, effective governance, monitoring, and sufficient finance.
Ambition must also be matched by resources. The new assessments estimate that around $16 billion is needed each year for marine protection under the 30% target, compared with only around $1.8 billion currently spent. Without the resources to manage them, protected areas risk remaining protected on paper rather than in practice.
As leaders gather at the United Nations General Assembly in New York, ocean protection should be part of discussions about climate resilience, food security, and economic stability. COP17 next month in Armenia will soon provide another opportunity for governments to confront where progress is falling furthest behind.
In 2019, I spoke from beneath the Indian Ocean because I wanted world leaders to understand that we could not leave the environmental problems we have created for another generation to solve.
That warning is more urgent today. But there are also reasons for hope. Countries have shown that ambitious conservation is possible. This June, French Polynesia announced an expansion that will bring 1.4 million square kilometers—around 30% of its waters—under full protection from extractive industries once implemented. Samoa and Portugal have also made meaningful increases in effective protection over the past year.
We now understand more about what effective protection requires. And with the High Seas Treaty in force, we have a powerful new means of safeguarding the ocean we all share.
The years between now and 2030 must be a turning point for ocean protection. We need to protect more of the ocean, protect it well, and seize the opportunity of the High Seas Treaty. If we do, we will not only safeguard biodiversity, but strengthen food security, climate resilience, and livelihoods for generations to come.

title: OpenAI wesprze Ukrainę w cyberochronie. Kijów dostanie narzędzie do walki z hakerami
content:
Dzięki Daybreak Kijów uzyska dostęp do zaawansowanego modelu GPT 5.6 Sol w wersji, która pozwala szybko wykrywać i usuwać luki w oprogramowaniu.
W 2025 r. ukraiński krajowy zespół reagowania na incydenty cybernetyczne CERT-UA odnotował prawie 6000 cyberataków. OpenAI ogłosiło współpracę z tą organizacją 23 września przy okazji Zgromadzenia Ogólnego ONZ w Nowym Jorku. — Ochrona infrastruktury cywilnej oznacza jej obronę zarówno przed atakami fizycznymi, jak i cyfrowymi, aby ludzie mogli nadal żyć, pracować i korzystać z niezbędnych usług — powiedział George Osborne, dyrektor ds. sztucznej inteligencji na rynkach międzynarodowych w OpenAI,
Wcześniej firma Anthropic, konkurująca z OpenAI, poinformowała, że jej system sztucznej inteligencji Claude został wykorzystany przez hakerów powiązanych z Rosją do ataków na ukraińskie organizacje. Hakerzy włamali się do skrzynek pocztowych co najmniej dwóch producentów komponentów do dronów, zaatakowali producenta dronów wojskowych oraz wykradli jego zestaw do tworzenia systemów wizyjnych.
Ukraina dysponuje już narzędziami opartymi na sztucznej inteligencji od innych konkurentów OpenAI — na przykład od Google — zauważył Jamie McColl, starszy pracownik naukowy Królewskiego Zjednoczonego Instytutu Badań Obronnych (RUSI).
W maju okazało się, że Ukraina korzysta z programów opartych na sztucznej inteligencji głównego dostawcy Pentagonu — giganta IT Palantir Technologies. Ówczesny minister obrony Mychajło Fedorow podkreślił, że w wyniku tej współpracy stworzono system szczegółowej analizy ataków powietrznych oraz wdrożono rozwiązania do pracy z dużymi zbiorami danych wywiadowczych. Ponadto technologie tej firmy są wykorzystywane przy planowaniu operacji typu "deep strike" — precyzyjnych, dalekosiężnych uderzeń Sił Zbrojnych Ukrainy na obiekty na tyłach Rosji.

title: Bittu Tabahi removes 585 kg garbage from Yamuna; CEO reacts: ‘Slap on administration’
content:
Surendra Singh Choudhary, better known as Bittu Tabahi, returned to the Yamuna riverbank on September 20 with a group of volunteers for a cleanup drive that lasted four and a half hours. Together, they collected around 585 kg of waste from the Delhi-NCR stretch of the river.
The 21-year-old student, who first gained attention for cleaning a garbage-filled river in his hometown Biaora in Madhya Pradesh, was praised online for the effort. Among those who applauded his work was Delhi-based entrepreneur Alok Jain, founder of WeekendInvesting.
Reacting to a post about the cleanup on X, Jain, an IIT Delhi alumnus, wrote, “Super wow and a tight slap on the local administration.” His post has since reached more than 50,000 people, with several users agreeing that volunteers like Choudhary are taking on work that should ordinarily be handled by civic authorities.
View this post on Instagram
One user wrote, “Huge applause! Shame also on citizens throwing garbage and waste here and there, everywhere.”
Another commented, “Why give a tight slap to the local administration???? They are helping Gen Z by doing nothing and giving our youth the opportunity to do this remarkable job of cleaning the river, and city themselves.”
“Tight slap on both govt and people who treat public places like garbage bin,” a third user wrote. Another tagged the Delhi chief minister and suggested, “Give him an official contract of cleaning Yamuna, he and his team are more dedicated and efficient than yours.”
Choudhary shared a video of the cleanup on September 22, showing volunteers picking up plastic, religious offerings and other waste scattered along the riverbank. “September 20, World Cleanup Day. Four and a half hours cleaning on the Yamuna bank, and together removed 585 kg of garbage,” he wrote in the caption.
“Flower garland, worship stuff, plastic, everything was scattered on the pier. People around came, handed out, and the whole riverbank was cleaned,” he added.
Choudhary said the campaign would continue for three days. He also plans to travel to other states to raise awareness about cleanliness and encourage people to take part in such efforts. As promised, two days after the Yamuna cleanup, Bittu Tabahi moved to Gurugram, where he and his team took up another cleanup drive at Khedki Daula.

title: [Research] Classification autism spectrum disorder associated genes through analysis of the intrinsic disorder in their protein products
content:
Abstract
Autism Spectrum Disorder (ASD) affects approximately 1–2% of children worldwide, posing challenges for healthcare, education, and families. While genetic factors play a key role, only a small subset of ASD-related genes has been identified with strong genetic evidence. This study introduces a machine learning-based approach to enhance the classification of ASD-associated genes by analyzing the intrinsically disordered regions (IDRs) of their protein products.
Using genetic data from the SFARI Gene database, 238 ASD-associated genes and 225 control genes were analyzed. Machine learning models, including artificial neural networks, were applied to classify ASD-related proteins based on IDR content and genetic patterns.
The model achieved 66% accuracy and an AUC of 0.73, successfully distinguishing ASD-associated genes from non-ASD genes. Functional enrichment analysis revealed that proteins with high IDR content (≥ 49%) were linked to behavior and cognition, while proteins with low IDR content (≤ 11%) were associated with memory function.
These findings suggest that IDRs play a crucial role in the functional specialization of ASD-associated proteins. This research demonstrates the potential of machine learning in ASD gene classification and provides insights into the biological mechanisms underlying ASD. Future studies could leverage these findings to improve genetic screening tools, diagnostics, and targeted therapies for ASD.

title: Protect This Place: Coastal Douglas-Fir Forest of Southwestern British Columbia
content:
The Place:
Morrell Nature Sanctuary is a 110-hectare (270-acre) preserve of coastal Douglas-fir forest in British Columbia that volunteers battle to keep safe from invasive species. The sanctuary is a shelter for a biodiverse ecosystem where fir coexist with massive red cedars, Garry oaks, and twisting, hard-as-stone arbutus trees with their shocking, ever-peeling red and pistachio-green trunks. The forest’s undergrowth is dominated by salal, Oregon grape, and ferns. But those are just a few of the more than 100 species of plants that provide a home for animals, including deer and bears. Ravens and barred owls regularly oversee our work.
Why it matters:
According to the Coastal Douglas-fir Conservation Partnership, this type of forest is the most at-risk zone in British Columbia, yet it contains the highest diversity of plant species in the province. Morrell Nature Sanctuary is a volunteer-led organization trying to maintain a small piece of this forest for all.
The threat:
The forest is in peril. Always creeping in from the edges or growing from bits dropped by birds are invasive Christmas-card perfect holly trees and very pretty, but toxic, daphne laurel. The open, rocky bluffs that the arbutus and Garry oaks favor are at risk of being taken over by Scotch broom. Local lore attributes the broom plague to a sentimental Scot who planted a few seeds to remind him of home. Now the broom has taken over any disturbed (literally and metaphorically) location across large swathes of southwestern British Columbia. It runs rampant up hydro lines, along trails and ditches, and in lots clearcut and then abandoned by developers. We curse the homesick Scot even as we grudgingly admire the bright yellow blooms in late spring.
It’s not just the sanctuary volunteers who engage in the Sisyphean labor of cutting blooming broom as close to the ground as possible. Many groups work to eradicate it, worrying the highly flammable, toxic bush will kill the native species and fuel a forest fire. It is dangerously everywhere.
The invasive-fighting volunteers have heard the arguments. Isn’t it natural evolution to let plants grow as they wish? That’s hard to believe if you witness the monoculture left under the canopy if you let daphne laurel grow at will. Isn’t it a waste of time? I can’t tell you how gratifying it is to liberate an arbutus from a surround of broom and know that even if you need to come back to cut baby broom next year, the arbutus is free for now. Parts of the sanctuary are close to pristine, where breathing is easier for everyone — and that can’t possibly be a waste of time or labor.
So we persist against the holly, daphne laurel, and broom while occasionally tackling other problematic plants in our neck of the woods: Periwinkle, English ivy (homesick settlers take note!) and Himalayan blackberry have also taken root.
My place in this place:
Of all the invasive plants, it’s the blackberry I find most difficult — and not just because of its vicious, rope-thick cane and brambles. There’s actually very little of it in the sanctuary, but when I occasionally come across it, I morph into a blackberry terminator, lasering in on the plant as I approach for the kill.
My technique involves clipping back as much of the vine and cane that I can until the roots are exposed, which I pull out of the ground with specially designed “puller-bears.” These heavy contraptions are very useful for pinching around the base of a plant and then slowly levering the roots out of the ground. They’re indispensable for clearing daphne laurel and smaller holly trees, which will regrow if cut. But never use a puller-bear on broom: You’ll just disturb the soil and create the perfect nursery for thousands of dormant broom seeds to sprout. It’s better to cut blooming broom off at the base, which will likely kill it.
But back to the blackberries. In the sanctuary I gleefully eradicate them. It’s when I leave that problems arise, as I wrestle with my hypocritical lust for a perfectly ripe blackberry. As soon as I touch a plump fruit, I know whether I should immediately pull it to my mouth or drop it in a bucket to freeze for delayed gratification over the winter. The ripe ones come to you willingly, almost falling into your hand as you caress them and then offer explosions of sweetness leaving a lingering, subtle, delicious tartness on your palate. There’s a reason “hints of blackberry” is often used to describe rich red wines.
As I walk to the sanctuary on summer mornings I assess the readiness of the crop, justifying my greediness with every step. They’ll still be there, taking over fields and ditches if I don’t eat them. And it’s free food! (Monetarily, at least.)
The coastal Douglas-fir ecosystem also has native trailing blackberries. Their fruits are smaller and sweeter, and many claim more delicious, than Himalayan blackberries. The trailing blackberry vine is also more delicate, and there’s no cane. While Himalayan blackberries would make an extremely effective defense against invaders, trailing blackberries allow animals to move through and coexist with salal and Oregon grape. Nonnative blackberries grow prolifically, not allowing anything else to grow and even competing with broom in disturbed sites. I believe it’s the alpha blackberry that will win out.
Have I mentioned the thorns the size of tacks that tear at your clothes, sometimes piercing the armor you donned before heading out on the hunt? For a month or so every summer the invasive blackberries dare you to come and get ’em if you’re brave enough to try. It’s not a chore for the unprepared. No matter the weather, you have to wear thick clothing and closed-toe shoes, if not boots. Mesh-topped running shoes won’t last a minute. The wise bring hand clippers to carve out a relatively safe space to pick. My husband carries an old broomstick with a bent nail banged into one end, which he uses to snag berry-laden branches and pull them within reach. He favors cutting his way in where others dare not go and picking in one spot. I wear a thick work glove on my non-picking hand to maneuver fruit nearer as I skim along the surface of the brambles. We’ve enviously watched seasoned warriors lean ladders against three-meter-high blackberry hedges to get at the ones the rest of us can’t reach.
My love of blackberries illustrates the issue at hand. Many invasive plants were originally planted in gardens because they’re pretty or taste good. I, along with everyone else, need to tamp down our selfish need for plants that don’t belong here. Inevitably as I enter the sanctuary, my mouth stained a deep purple, I relax because it’s always cooler there when it’s hot out. On rainy days the towering canopy gives protection. I stop and breathe and know that given the choice of this or blackberries, I will choose the forest every time. That’s what we are fighting to protect.
Who’s protecting it now:
Volunteers. In addition to the Morrell nature sanctuary, volunteers with organizations such as BroomBusters are working in the region to eradicate invasive species, Scotch broom in particular.
What this place needs:
The smallest actions, such as ripping out an invasive plant as one walks by, can quickly add up, clearing areas remarkably effectively. But local government leaders also need to step in and recognize the threat posed by invasive plants. The wildfires should terrify us all and spur action to legislate the removal of plants such as Scotch broom or fine those who don’t take action. Another step is to make the disposal of invasive plants easier. Right now, it costs us to take bags of pulled or cut plants for disposal; we need support, not barriers.
Lessons from the fight:
A small group of mostly retired people working a few hours a week can make a surprisingly big difference. But we Morrell volunteers are only working on a tiny piece of the landscape. If more people started working a bit more broadly, I believe much more of the forest could be protected. For example, I regularly walk through a Nanaimo park that’s choking on invasive plants. Holly and daphne are everywhere, and the cedars and firs are covered in ivy. Yet it’s obvious where people have stepped in to eradicate the interlopers, leaving pockets of forest in a clean state. It can be done.
Learn more:
To find out more about the Morrell Nature Sanctuary, visit their website or follow them on Facebook.
To see the work of another invasive fighting volunteer organization, with inspiring examples of small groups who made big impacts, visit the BroomBuster’s website.
To learn more about the coastal Douglas-fir ecosystem visit: https://www.cdfcp.ca/about-the-cdfcp/.

title: Na stopzetting veldcross in Essen: "Ook organisatie Sluitingsprijs Oostmalle is complexer geworden"
content:
Het wordt steeds moeilijker om een veldcross te organiseren, zowel financieel als praktisch. Dat zegt de organisatie van de Sluitingsprijs Oostmalle, na het nieuws dat de verlieslijdende cyclocross in Essen ermee ophoudt. In Oostmalle is het een lokale wielervereniging die erin slaagt om zelf nog genoeg sponsors te vinden. Toch is het allemaal veel complexer en duurder geworden, getuigt organisator Mon Leys.
Na stopzetting veldcross in Essen: "Ook organisatie Sluitingsprijs Oostmalle is complexer geworden"
De Wielersupportersclub van Oostmalle organiseert nog steeds helemaal zelfstandig de Internationale Sluitingsprijs Oostmalle, ook al wordt dat steeds moeilijker en duurder. Dat zegt organisator Mon Leys naar aanleiding van het stopzetten van de veldcross in Essen.
De Wielersupportersclub organiseert de Sluitingsprijs al minstens 35 jaar. Andere crossen in de provincie worden georganiseerd door grote sporteventorganisatoren zoals Golazo of Flanders Classics. De Oostmalse supportersclub doet dat, nog als enige in de provincie, op eigen kracht en met steun van de gemeente.
Financiële uitdaging
Het draaiende houden van de organisatie is volgens Mon Leys elk jaar een uitdaging. "Praktisch gezien moet onze organisatie ervoor zorgen dat er voldoende opvolging en verjonging komt", zegt hij. Naast de praktische kant moet de club ook een verdienmodel uitbouwen om de prijzen, organisatiekosten, startgelden van de renners en inrichtingskosten te betalen.
Zonder tv-uitzending halen we ons sponsorbudget niet
Mon Leys, organisator Sluitingsprijs Oostmalle
Sponsoring is daarbij cruciaal. Of een cross op televisie te zien is, speelt een grote rol bij het aantrekken van sponsors. "Zonder tv-uitzending halen we het sponsorbudget niet dat wij voor ogen hebben", zegt Leys. De club heeft de voorbije jaren een vast sponsorbestand opgebouwd, al vallen er soms sponsors weg en komen er nieuwe bij. Voor dit jaar verwacht de club enkele nieuwe sponsors.
Meer materiaal nodig
De organisatie van een cross is ingrijpend veranderd. Vroeger volstonden een paaltje, een lintje en een kleine tent van 4 op 6 meter. "Vandaag zijn een aankomst- en startportiek nodig, samen met nadars en afsluitingen om het parcours veilig af te bakenen."
Ook de tenten zijn groter geworden: in plaats van kleine tentjes gaat het nu om tenten van 60 à 70 meter lang en 20 meter breed voor genodigden en supporters," zegt Mon Leys. De club werkt daarvoor samen met de gemeente Malle, maar moet ook veel materiaal huren, en dat kost allemaal veel geld.
Vipformule
De vipformule bij de cross is de voorbije jaren ook veranderd. Vroeger was er een zittende vipformule waarbij mensen konden tafelen tijdens de cross, naast een losse formule met drank en snacks. Volgens Leys is het moeilijker geworden om daar veel geld voor te vragen. En dus hebben ze de prijzen aangepast.

title: Development and Validation of a Machine Learning-Based Model for Predicting All-Cause Mortality Risk in Patients With Type 2 Diabetes Mellitus Combined With Hypertension: National Cohort Study.
content: Type 2 diabetes mellitus (T2DM) combined with hypertension significantly increases mortality risk, yet accurate risk prediction models remain limited. We aimed to develop and validate machine learning-based models to predict all-cause mortality in patients with T2DM and hypertension. We analyzed data from the National Health and Nutrition Examination Survey from 1999 to 2018 linked with mortality data up to December 31, 2019. Adult participants (aged ≥20 years) with concurrent T2DM and hypertension were included. Five machine learning algorithms were developed and compared: random forest, light gradient boosting machine, decision tree, extreme gradient boosting, and logistic regression. Model performance was evaluated using area under the curve (AUC), calibration plots, and decision curve analysis. A total of 2428 participants were included (mean age 62.05, SE 0.33 years; n=1218, 50.15% female). During a median follow-up of 6.75 (IQR 4.20-8.90) years, among the 2428 patients, 719 (29.6%) deaths occurred. The random forest model demonstrated superior performance (AUC=0.873, 95% CI 0.856-0.891) compared to light gradient boosting machine (AUC=0.785), decision tree (AUC=0.732), extreme gradient boosting (AUC=0.792), and logistic regression (AUC=0.783). Key predictive features included age, race, chronic kidney disease, BMI, and blood urea nitrogen. The model exhibited excellent calibration and clinical utility across various risk thresholds. Our machine learning-based model provides accurate all-cause mortality prediction for patients with T2DM and hypertension, potentially supporting clinical decision-making and risk stratification in this high-risk population.

title: Kourweogo/Reboisement : Les ressortissants de Tangseghin plantent une centaine d’arbres pour reverdir l’école de Rana
content:
BURKINA-KOURWEOGO-NIOU-REBOISEMENT
Kourweogo/Reboisement : Les ressortissants de Tangseghin plantent une centaine d’arbres pour reverdir l’école de Rana
Niou, 19 sept. 2026 (AIB)- Les ressortissants du village de Tangseghin, dans la commune de Niou, ont organisé, le samedi 19 septembre 2026, une campagne de reboisement à l’école primaire publique de Rana, avec la mise en terre d’une centaine de plants pour reverdir l’établissement et améliorer le cadre de vie des élèves.
L’activité s’est déroulée avec la participation de la population, d’élèves, du personnel de l’école ainsi que de ressortissants de Rana venus de plusieurs localités du pays.
Pour le représentant des ressortissants, Ibrahim Sawadogo, cette initiative répond à un besoin réel de l’établissement.
« C’est un acte que nous avons jugé nécessaire, au regard du manque d’ombre dans l’établissement. Nous souhaitons contribuer à améliorer le cadre scolaire des élèves et à protéger davantage l’environnement », a-t-il indiqué.
Pour lui, les plants que nous avons mis en terre sont tous à l’abri des animaux puisqu’ils bénéficient tous d’une grille de protection.
Le directeur de l’école primaire publique de Rana, Mahamoudou Sawadogo, a salué l’initiative, estimant qu’elle contribuera à offrir davantage d’espaces ombragés aux élèves et aussi à protéger et à sauvegarder notre milieu de vie.
« Nous prenons la résolution de protéger et d’entretenir ce bosquet pour le bonheur du village en général et de nos apprenants en particulier », a-t-il déclaré.
De son côté, le président du conseil d’école, Adama Sawadogo, a remercié les initiateurs pour avoir pensé à une telle activité, qui selon lui, va contribuer à améliorer les conditions de travail des enseignants et d’apprentissage des élèves.
« Nous allons, avec nos enfants, prendre soin de ces plants, à en assurer l’entretien et la protection des plants, afin de garantir leur survie et de pérenniser les acquis de cette campagne de reboisement », a également soutenu le président du conseil.
Cette initiative qui est à sa première édition a été salué par les notables du quartier. Ils ont souhaité la pérennisation de ses rencontres, qui pour eux sert de cadre de retrouvailles et de renforcement des liens de famille.

title: In Gujarat, Sahjeevan Works with Pastoralist Communities to Preserve Prairies that are Essential to Biodiversity
content:
For over 30 years, Sahjeevan has empowered India’s pastoralist communities to secure grazing rights, conserve rare livestock breeds, and build self-sustaining livelihoods in Gujarat.
India’s pastoralist communities have found a steady partner in Sahjeevan, a nonprofit based in Gujarat’s Kachchh region. For more than 30 years, the organization has worked alongside herders who move cattle, buffalo, sheep, goats, and camels across some of the country’s harshest terrain. Its name combines two words meaning togetherness and life, a fitting description of decades spent building trust in the field.
Sahjeevan’s approach rests on a simple belief. Communities that have shaped a working relationship with their landscape are often best placed to protect it. That idea has guided the group’s work since it began in Kachchh, then expanded into Saurashtra and, more recently, across India.
Much of that work centers on the Banni grassland, one of Asia’s largest tropical grasslands. Pastoralists known as Maldharis have grazed cattle and buffalo here for generations. Their herds include the Banni buffalo, a hardy breed known for high milk yields and long grazing distances at night.
Sahjeevan’s reach now stretches across six distinct terrains within Kachchh and Saurashtra. These include grassland, thorn-scrub forest, mangroves, and both rain-fed and irrigated farmland. Each terrain supports different pastoralist communities and livestock adapted to those specific conditions.
Fencing, invasive weeds, and shifting management rules have squeezed the grassland in recent decades. An invasive tree introduced decades ago to curb salinity spread aggressively, crowding out native forage grasses. Herders say these changes threaten both their livelihoods and the ecosystem they help maintain.
Sahjeevan has helped pastoralist communities respond by turning to India’s Forest Rights Act. The 2006 law lets communities claim formal rights over forest and grazing land they have traditionally used. Since 2012, herder groups in Banni have filed claims covering thousands of square kilometers of grazing land.
Communities that file these claims form management committees to oversee the land. These committees draft plans to regenerate grasslands, remove invasive species, and protect wildlife. Progress has been uneven, with some approved claims still awaiting formal government titles.
Elsewhere in Gujarat, Sahjeevan supports herders raising other distinctive breeds suited to extreme conditions. Fakirani Jat herders in coastal Kachchh keep Kharai camels, a rare breed able to swim several kilometers to graze on mangrove leaves. Rabari and Jat communities in other areas raise camels, goats, and sheep across desert and thorn-scrub terrain.
Beyond grazing rights, Sahjeevan helps these pastoralist communities diversify how they earn a living. Programs support wool and milk value chains, veterinary care, and market connections for non-bovine dairy products. Partnerships with dairy cooperatives aim to bring pastoral milk into wider markets while keeping herding economically viable.
Much of this work happens through community-based organizations that Sahjeevan helped establish. The oldest of these, formed in 2008, now counts more than 1,800 animal breeders among its members. These groups give herders a collective voice in decisions that affect their grazing lands and livestock.
Sahjeevan also engages with government agencies and courts to advocate for pastoralist recognition. In one case, a herder group took legal action to remove agricultural encroachments from the Banni grassland. As the [Forest Rights Act](https://tribal.nic.in/fra.aspx) states, communities that gain recognition also take on responsibility for conserving biodiversity and managing forest resources sustainably.
Sahjeevan organizes this broad effort around three interconnected approaches. It equips pastoralist communities with information and market linkages, helps them build lasting institutions, and advocates for supportive policy at the state and national level. Together, these approaches aim to give herders a stronger say in decisions that shape their futures.
Three decades on, Sahjeevan’s work continues to expand beyond Kachchh into new landscapes across India. Its core belief remains unchanged: pastoralist communities who understand their land are essential partners in conserving it. That partnership offers a model for balancing biodiversity conservation with the livelihoods of people who have sustained these landscapes for generations, long before conservation became a formal discipline.

title: A Herd of 40 Life-Size Bison Puppets Will Stampede Through New York This Weekend to Honor Indigenous History and Resilience
content:
A Herd of 40 Life-Size Bison Puppets Will Stampede Through New York This Weekend to Honor Indigenous History and Resilience
The massive bovines, each maneuvered by three puppeteers, will roam through Lower Manhattan and Brooklyn
Dozens of life-size bison puppets—made this summer with steel, plywood, burlap and paper—will roam the streets of New York City this weekend as part of a free art spectacle that honors both the mammal and the Indigenous communities who have revered and stewarded their herds since time immemorial.
The two-day public exhibition, “Return of the Buffalo: Tatanka Owe Akupi,” celebrates the animal’s journey from near extinction in the late 19th century to its gradual repopulation across the American prairie. The event, whose Lakota name translates roughly to “Trail of the Buffalo,” will feature two separate routes, one through Lower Manhattan and another through Brooklyn.
Poetry readings, live music, ceremonies and dancing will complement the roving stampede and contextualize the bison’s role in American and pre-American history.
“The land that we call America today has been here for far more than 250 years, and this production memorializes that,” Amir Nizar Zuabi, the event’s creator, says in a statement. “The United States presents great hope, promise and potential, as well as a history of destruction and loss. In this moment, we have a civic duty to come together as a community of global citizens to usher in a new chapter in America’s history, one that learns from its past, with empathy and respect for the land and all humans living on it.”
The event will begin this evening in front of the National Museum of the American Indian with a performance by elders from the Lenape and Lakota tribes. As the herd roams, it will make more than a dozen stops alongside civic and cultural leaders at historic locations. Actors Sam Waterston, Rosario Dawson and Susan Sarandon are among the more well-known celebrities joining in the walks. Members of different tribes will share knowledge and stories with observers.
The stars of the event are the 40 life-size bison, each operated by three volunteer puppeteers: two inside, controlling the rear legs and head—which weighs 40 pounds alone—and one outside, serving as the bison’s eyes. Each bison’s movements were carefully choreographed over days of training, with particular emphasis on how to move and breathe both as an individual and as part of the herd. Several commands, such as “gallop” and “regroup,” will be issued in Xhosa and Arabic, the native languages of the event’s creators. A total of 150 performers will steer the performance.
“It’s not every day you get to be part of an entire herd of bison and charge through the streets of New York and bring awareness to, you know, the meaning of it all,” Craig Leo, the event’s puppetry director, tells the New York Times’ Laura Collins-Hughes. “So it happens once in your life.”
The puppets were designed by the South American company Ukwanda Puppets—which has built puppets for “The Herds,” another traveling public art exhibition—and constructed in New York City, at St. Ann’s Warehouse.
Indigenous leaders were heavily involved in creating the bison, the exhibition’s choreography and the weekend’s resonant messaging. The story of Great Plains bison and tribes go hand in hand: In the mid-1800s, both were thriving across the American prairie. But, as John Thomas, a Lenape elder of the Delaware Tribe of Indians, tells amNY’s Renee DeLorenzo, “you kill a buffalo, you kill an Indian.” Violence wrought by colonial settlers and hunters pushed Indigenous people, their culture and the animal they relied on to the brink of extinction.
Once numbered in the tens of millions, fewer than 1,000 bison remained by the 1890s. Today, roughly 500,000 live across the United States.
“We are inviting New Yorkers to reflect and appreciate nature, our land, and our power to heal and renew,” Susan Feldman, the artistic director of St. Ann’s Warehouse, says in a statement. “The story of the American buffalo reminds us of the near extinction of a majestic creature, and it acknowledges a magnificent human effort to rewild them. It represents the worst of us and the best of us.”

title: U Federaciji BiH proširena lista lijekova za teške bolesti, među kojima su i maligne

U Federaciji BiH proširena lista lijekova za teške bolesti, među kojima su i maligne
Kako su ukazali, na listu lijekova Fonda solidarnosti uvrštene su terapije lijekovima pembrolizumab i atezolizumab, čime se proširuju mogućnosti liječenja pacijenata oboljelih od više teških malignih bolesti, u skladu sa stručnim medicinskim kriterijima.
Ova odluka dio je, kako su ocijenili, kontinuiranog povećanja ulaganja u Fond solidarnosti. Za Fond je u protekle četiri godine osigurano 296 miliona KM, odnosno više od 60 miliona KM nego što je za istu namjenu izdvojeno, kako tvrde, tokom prethodnih osam godina.
Vlada je donijela i odluku o dopuni liste lijekova obaveznog zdravstvenog osiguranja lijekom natrij oksibat, namijenjenim pacijentima s narkolepsijom praćenom katapleksijom.
"Uvrštavanje novih lijekova na liste znači više mogućnosti za liječenje ljudi koji se suočavaju s teškim bolestima. Naša je odgovornost da zajedno sa strukom pratimo razvoj medicine i stvarne potrebe pacijenata. Za svakog čovjeka koji čeka terapiju najvažnije je da je dobije na vrijeme i da mu bude dostupno liječenje koje mu može pomoći. Zato nastavljamo stvarati uslove da savremene terapije budu dostupne što većem broju pacijenata kojima su potrebne", izjavio je federalni premijer Nermin Nikšić (SDP).

title: ACP, state wildlife agencies launch guidelines for utility-scale solar development
content:
ACP, state wildlife agencies launch guidelines for utility-scale solar development
Utility-scale solar, one of the most rapidly deployed and affordable energy sources, can also provide habitat benefits for certain species. Developing solar on large swaths of land, however, may also adversely impact wildlife and their habitats without proper planning and communication. Recognizing the need to balance development with wildlife protection, American Clean Power Association (ACP) worked with Association of Fish and Wildlife Agencies (AFWA) and Energy and Wildlife Action Coalition (EWAC) to develop the National Utility-Scale Solar Wildlife Guidelines.
The conservation considerations and priorities vary from region to region and state to state and keeping track of them can be daunting. However, the guidelines stress that by considering wildlife and habitat early on and then throughout the project, unintended impacts can be avoided. Impacts on wildlife discovered late in the process may not only harm the ecosystem but can cause costly delays for solar projects.
An example of such a delay is the Soda Mountain Solar Project, the development of which was halted more than a decade ago when local officials in San Bernardino County in California voted to block the development, citing environmental impacts on federal lands, specifically raising concerns about the migratory paths of desert bighorn sheep. Just recently the California Energy Commission issued a recommendation to move the project forward.
“State fish and wildlife agencies are entrusted with protecting our natural resources for generations to come,” said Paul Johansen, past president of the Association of Fish & Wildlife Agencies and chief of the Wildlife Resources Section for the West Virginia Division of Natural Resources. “These guidelines show how agencies and solar developers can work together, using sound science and early communication to meet our energy goals while safeguarding the fish and wildlife the public cherishes.”
The guidelines include a Communication Framework for Solar Energy Project Proponents and State Fish and Wildlife Agencies that state agencies can use in science-based decision making, while also being flexible about site-specific issues and individual state processes.
“This balanced framework reflects that commitment and provides a model for how industry and agencies can work together to address complex conservation and infrastructure challenges as energy demand rises nationally,” said John Anderson, executive director of the Energy and Wildlife Action Coalition.
As the guidelines are voluntary and designed to improve communication between parties, they are not intended to replace or preempt existing federal, state, or local fish and wildlife-related authorities, permitting requirements, or established review procedures. Instead, they are expected to complement existing processes and support site assessment, project development, construction and operations in areas where formal wildlife-related permitting or review processes may be limited or non-existent.
The guidelines address six stages of solar project planning, development and operations, with a summary of the approach, communications triggers, and key considerations included for each:
1. Relationship building (between the developer and state agency)
2. Preliminary area evaluation
3. Site characterization and design
4. Construction
5. Operations
6. Decommissioning
Topics covered include species of interest, habitat connectivity, seasonality of certain wildlife considerations, vegetation management, fencing, voluntary conservation opportunities, and beneficial effects of solar projects. There is also consideration of the priorities of state fish and wildlife agencies. Furthermore, the framework takes into account potential limitations on developers due to other factors involved in project siting and design.
ACP represents energy storage, wind, utility-scale solar, and transmission companies and is committed to “meeting America’s energy and national security goals and building our economy with fast-growing, low-cost, and reliable domestic power.”
The EWAC assists members in managing natural resources issues associated with the development, generation, transmission, or sale of electricity. The organization’s primary mission is to “promote public policies that are based on sound science, protective of wildlife and natural resources, practical, and efficient.” AFWA represents North America’s fish and wildlife agencies to advance sound, science-based management and conservation of fish and wildlife and their habitats in the public interest.

title: Famous Maremma guardian dog penguin project under threat
content:
Fears for survival of Warrnambool's little penguins and famous Maremma guardian dog project
For 20 years, a penguin colony on a small island by the Victorian coastal city of Warrnambool has been protected from fox attacks by a team of guardian dogs.
Featured in the 2015 children's film Oddball and colloquially known as The Warrnambool Method by conservationists, the world's first penguin protection technique has diminished in recent years.
Safety concerns about erosion and the deep waters surrounding the island have led the volunteer-run project to scale back.
Trained Maremma sheep dogs once lived on the island for weeks at a time during the little penguin breeding season, but it has been two years since a dog has stayed the night.
The dogs were introduced in 2006, after foxes nearly hunted the penguin colony to extinction.
By 2016, the population had recovered from less than 10 penguins to 200.
Dave Williams, who started the Maremma dog project with a friend as a university student, said he feared the colony was now more vulnerable to being wiped out, but that it had become too dangerous for volunteers and dogs to reach the island.
"I'd like to think that we'll always have penguins at Middle Island and it's something that Warrnambool can be proud of," Mr Williams said.
"When we started this, there was less than 10 penguins, this project is something that the community has supported and driven.
"I think it'd be a terrible shame if we lost that."
Middle Island is about 150 metres from shore, and for years volunteers waded through a knee-deep channel to handle the dogs and count how many penguins were arriving to nest, but now the water is too deep.
Population a mystery
Over the past six years, despite occasional visits to the island in good weather, the health of the colony's population has become a mystery.
"Ultimately, if you haven't got eyes on the ground, you've got no idea what's happening out there," Mr Williams said.
The dogs are still taken to the nearby beaches to leave their scent, as a warning to foxes, but he said it's not the same as having a resident guard dog there every night.
"That thousand-year-old methodology of dogs keeping foxes away still works,"he said.
"It's not particularly safe for people or dogs now."
Marine scientist and former Middle Island project coordinator Patricia Corbett said the channel around the island has been too deep to cross for population counts for years.
"We know there are penguins on the island, but we really don't know how many," Dr Corbett said.
"We had a really big erosion event.
"For the last few years, it hasn't gotten any shallower than about chest level or waist level at the lowest, and there's a really strong current; it's not safe."
Rocky reefs have also made it difficult to reach the island by boat.
In the last breeding season, counts were only held on only a few occasions, when conditions allowed, and not a single penguin was sighted.
Infrastructure troubles
The project also relied on a wooden boardwalk built in 2002 to prevent the dogs from crushing burrows or jumping off the island, but it has fallen into disrepair.
Warrnambool City Council natural environment and sustainability coordinator Justin Harzmeyer said the council was not planning on purchasing new dogs to replace the current guardians as they age, because they could only be trained on the island.
Mr Harzmeyer said the council was looking into whether upgrades could continue the project in future.
"Having the Maremmas, we're not legislated to it, but it's a nice thing to do, and we've been doing it for 20 years," Mr Harzmeyer said.
"If the guardian side of the project were to finish up, there'd still be that [educational and tourist] interest and there'll be a legacy of the project."
Environmental threats
Dr Corbett said she was hopeful the channel's rough conditions would stop foxes from crossing to the island.
The last fox attack was in 2019, but Dr Corbett said that without monitoring, it was hard to know whether there had been another.
Little penguins on Deen Maar Island, near Port Fairy, have been found with aluminium and titanium in their feathers, and seals have been found with high levels of PFAS in their digestive systems.
Dr Corbett said they had not been able to test the Middle Island colony, but she suspected similar pollution could harm them.
She said heatwaves and severe weather events associated with climate change could disrupt their breeding.
"Whenever we have an increase in temperature above normal for five days or more, this can really stress the penguins," she said.
Fears of H5 bird flu outbreak
Unlike colonies in Phillip Island and St Kilda, the little penguins at Middle Island were not being vaccinated for the H5 strain of bird flu.
Every spring, the penguins share Middle Island with a colony of shearwaters, a migratory bird that usually arrives in late September and October to breed.
Dr Corbett said the colony was very healthy, with at least 300 birds.
She said this would ordinarily be a good sign for the local ecosystem, but if the shearwaters spread bird flu, there likely wouldn't be enough penguins to keep the colony alive if a mass death event occurred.
"Particularly with the shearwaters arriving soon, where we know that they're coming from areas that do have bird flu and they're in very close quarters with the penguins, there definitely is potential for big impact on the colony," she said.
"It's quite challenging, as it's great that there's obviously vaccination programs happening at St Kilda and Phillip Island, but we just have to wait and see what happens."
New technology
Warrnambool Coastcare Landcare Network, the main operator of the Maremma project, have purchased cameras to install on the island this breeding season.
Dave Williams said remote monitoring would never be enough to truly understand the penguins' health.
Mr Williams is now the coordinator of the Eastern Maar Aboriginal Corporation's sea country team — the custodians of the waters around Warrnambool.
The sea country team have flown drones over the island since the outbreak of bird flu, and found a few dead birds.
"Almost everything we saw was alive, there were a couple of dead terns," he said.
"We don't really know [if the birds died from bird flu], until we are finding those mass mortalities.
"We're worried about all sorts of these discrete populations and colonies, that bird flu could put an end to."
Future unknown
Mr Williams said in an ideal world, he wanted to return to hands-on monitoring of the penguins and get the dogs back on the island.
"Everybody's sort of scratching their heads about how this project moves forward," he said.
"Foxes can swim, and they've been observed swimming out there in some pretty inclement conditions.
"It might be that another fox does find its way out there again — once it realises there's a whole bunch of easy tucker out there, it will take that risk again."

title: Effectiveness of Telehealth Care Interventions for Women's Mental Health During and After the COVID-19 Pandemic: Systematic Review and Meta-Analysis.
content: The COVID-19 pandemic has increased telemental health interventions. However, evidence of effectiveness in improving women's mental health outcomes, acceptability, and user satisfaction remains fragmented. This study examined the effectiveness of telehealth interventions in alleviating depression, anxiety, and stress in women during and after the pandemic and descriptively summarized the acceptability of and satisfaction with these interventions. This systematic review and meta-analysis compared telemental health interventions with control conditions (waitlists or standard care) for women experiencing anxiety, depression, or stress. Databases (PubMed/MEDLINE, Embase, Web of Science, PsycINFO, and Cochrane Central Register of Controlled Trials) were searched through March 19, 2026. Eligible studies evaluated interventions in women aged 18 to 64 years (≥80% female participants and female-specific outcomes) and included randomized controlled trials (RCTs), nonrandomized trials, and observational studies with ≥5 participants using outcome measures. Random-effects meta-analyses were conducted for depression, anxiety, and stress using RCT data. Risk of bias was assessed using Cochrane tools and certainty of evidence using Grading of Recommendations, Assessment, Development and Evaluation. Fifty-seven studies (N=13,457) from 24 countries, reported the effectiveness, acceptability, and satisfaction with telehealth interventions. Meta-analysis of 23 studies (n=3269) demonstrated significant benefits of telehealth interventions for depression, anxiety, and stress. Depression showed the greatest improvements, with a moderate reduction in symptoms (Hedges g=-0.56, 95% CI -0.86 to -0.26; P<.001), followed by anxiety (small to moderate reduction; Hedges g=-0.45, 95% CI -0.62 to -0.28; P<.001). Stress showed a smaller effect (Hedges g=-0.25, 95% CI -0.47 to -0.04; P=.02), indicating modest benefits. Heterogeneity was high, with 95% prediction intervals of -1.97 to 0.84, -1.11 to 0.21, and -0.98 to 0.40 for depression, anxiety, and stress, respectively. Subgroup analyses favored telehealth over waitlist and standard care for depression (waitlist: Hedges g=-0.60, 95% CI -0.86 to -0.33; standard care: Hedges g=-0.57, 95% CI -1.11 to -0.02; both P<.001) and anxiety (waitlist: Hedges g=-0.47, 95% CI -0.68 to -0.25; standard care: Hedges g=-0.52, 95% CI -0.80 to -0.25; both P<.001). Insufficient studies were available to evaluate stress in subgroup analyses. Treatment effects remained significant in female-only and predominantly female samples. Evidence certainty was downgraded due to heterogeneity, risk of bias, and methodological limitations. This is the first systematic review and meta-analysis focused on telemental health interventions for women. Telehealth was associated with moderate, small to moderate, and modest reductions in depression, anxiety, and stress, respectively, with benefits across female-only and predominantly female samples. Moderate to high heterogeneity in average effects (CIs), wide distributions of effects across settings (prediction intervals), and risk of bias resulted in moderate certainty of evidence. Overall, telehealth is a scalable approach for improving access to mental health care for women, although high-quality research is needed to strengthen the evidence base.

Bắc Ninh là thành phố thứ 9 từ ngày mai
Từ ngày 20/9, Bắc Ninh trở thành thành phố trực thuộc trung ương, định hướng trở thành đô thị xanh, thông minh, hiện đại, mang bản sắc văn hóa Kinh Bắc.
Sáng 19/9, tỉnh Bắc Ninh tổ chức lễ công bố Nghị quyết của Quốc hội thành lập thành phố Bắc Ninh và đón nhận huân chương Lao động hạng nhất. Bắc Ninh là thành phố thứ 9 của cả nước, được thành lập trên cơ sở nguyên trạng diện tích tự nhiên 4.700 km2, dân số gần 4 triệu người của tỉnh hiện nay.
Sau khi sáp nhập với Bắc Giang từ giữa năm 2025, Bắc Ninh có trung tâm hành chính đặt tại phường Bắc Giang. Năm 2025, GRDP của tỉnh tăng 10,27%, đứng thứ 5 cả nước; thu hút 5,73 tỷ USD vốn FDI, xếp thứ hai sau TP HCM.
Theo nghị quyết của Quốc hội, TP Bắc Ninh được định hướng trở thành đô thị xanh, thông minh, hiện đại, mang bản sắc văn hóa Kinh Bắc; lấy khoa học, công nghệ và đổi mới sáng tạo làm động lực tăng trưởng. Địa phương sẽ phát triển công nghiệp công nghệ cao, hướng tới hình thành trung tâm điện tử, bán dẫn, sản xuất vi mạch và trí tuệ nhân tạo hàng đầu cả nước và khu vực.
Phát biểu tại buổi lễ, Tổng Bí thư, Chủ tịch nước Tô Lâm đã lược lại lịch sử, những dấu ấn của Bắc Ninh. Nhắc đến Bắc Ninh - Kinh Bắc là nhắc đến một vùng đất có chiều sâu hiếm có về lịch sử và văn hóa, gắn với tín ngưỡng thờ Kinh Dương Vương, Luy Lâu cổ kính, nơi phát tích của Vương triều Lý, mở ra thời kỳ rực rỡ của nền văn minh Đại Việt. Nói đến Bắc Ninh là nhớ đến Nam quốc sơn hà bên sông Như Nguyệt, thành Xương Giang, Yên Thế và những trận không chiến với không quân Mỹ trên bầu trời Hà Bắc...
Kinh Bắc là vùng đất học tiêu biểu, trong gần một nghìn năm khoa cử có tới 1/3 tiến sĩ, trạng nguyên cả nước và gần 700 vị đỗ đại khoa. Đây cũng là quê hương của nhiều bậc hiền tài, danh nhân lịch sử, văn hóa, quân sự và nhiều nhà cách mạng tiền bối của Đảng; là cội nguồn của nhiều lễ hội, nghệ thuật dân gian và làng nghề truyền thống, đặc biệt là những làn điệu dân ca quan họ mượt mà đằm thắm, đã được UNESCO công nhận là di sản văn hóa phi vật thể đại diện của nhân loại.
"Bắc Ninh là một trong những đại diện tiêu biểu của nền văn hiến Việt Nam. Nền văn hiến ấy vẫn đang nảy nở, phát triển, hun đúc nên phẩm chất rất quý của người Kinh Bắc như tinh thần hiếu học, trọng tri thức, trọng nhân nghĩa, có ý chí vươn lên và luôn hướng tới những giá trị cao đẹp", Tổng Bí thư, Chủ tịch nước nói.
Thời gian tới, Tổng Bí thư, Chủ tịch nước đề nghị TP Bắc Ninh xác lập tầm nhìn dài hạn và mô hình phát triển riêng, định vị rõ vai trò trong 20-30 năm tới. Địa phương cần xây dựng mô hình đô thị hiện đại, giàu bản sắc, cân bằng giữa công nghiệp, dịch vụ, sinh thái và chất lượng sống.
Người đứng đầu Đảng, Nhà nước lưu ý Bắc Ninh cần xây dựng nội lực kinh tế, từng bước làm chủ công nghệ và nâng cao vị trí trong chuỗi giá trị. Thành phố thu hút đầu tư có chọn lọc, hấp thụ công nghệ, tri thức và năng lực quản trị. Công nghiệp hỗ trợ cần thúc đẩy phát triển cùng với kết nối doanh nghiệp trong nước và khu vực đầu tư nước ngoài, đưa doanh nghiệp Việt Nam vào những khâu có giá trị cao.
"Sự phát triển của Bắc Ninh phải được thể hiện bằng năng lực công nghệ của chính mình, sự trưởng thành của doanh nghiệp trong nước và phần giá trị ngày càng lớn được tạo ra, giữ lại trên quê hương, tạo ra giá trị gia tăng cao hơn và đóng góp lớn hơn cho cả nước", ông nói.
Địa phương đồng thời tổ chức lại không gian phát triển, xây dựng đô thị xanh, thông minh, đáng sống. Bắc Ninh phải được quy hoạch như một chỉnh thể thống nhất, kết nối hài hòa công nghiệp, đô thị, dịch vụ, nông nghiệp, sinh thái và văn hóa; ưu tiên hạ tầng liên kết vùng và chuẩn bị đồng bộ kết nối với sân bay Gia Bình.
Con người, nguồn nhân lực chất lượng cao cần được phát triển gắn với sức mạnh văn hóa Kinh Bắc. Tổng Bí thư, Chủ tịch nước gợi ý địa phương có chính sách đủ mạnh để thu hút, trọng dụng kỹ sư, chuyên gia, nhà khoa học, nhà quản lý giỏi, từng bước hình thành đội ngũ nhân lực đủ năng lực tiếp nhận, làm chủ và sáng tạo công nghệ. Đồng thời, phải đưa quan họ, tranh Đông Hồ, làng nghề, di tích, truyền thống hiếu học và văn hóa cộng đồng vào đời sống hiện đại, biến di sản thành nguồn lực cho công nghiệp văn hóa, du lịch và sáng tạo.
Khi lên thành phố, Bắc Ninh cần nâng cao chất lượng giáo dục, y tế, nhà ở và dịch vụ thiết yếu, đặc biệt đối với công nhân, người lao động và các địa bàn còn khó khăn. "Kiên quyết không đánh đổi sức khỏe người dân, môi trường và tương lai các thế hệ lấy tăng trưởng trước mắt", ông nói.
TP Bắc Ninh phải là đô thị hiện đại, xanh, nhân văn, có nền công nghiệp công nghệ cao, có những doanh nghiệp Việt Nam đủ sức vươn ra thế giới, nhưng vẫn là "thành phố đậm đà hồn cốt và văn hóa Kinh Bắc".
Bí thư Thành ủy Bắc Ninh Nguyễn Hồng Thái bày tỏ "trở thành thành phố không phải là đích đến, đây chỉ là điểm khởi đầu cho một giai đoạn phát triển mới". "Hướng tới xây dựng TP Bắc Ninh xanh, thông minh, hiện đại, văn minh và giàu đẹp, mang đậm bản sắc văn hóa Kinh Bắc, đóng góp tích cực vào sự phát triển của vùng và cả nước", ông nói.
Với việc bổ sung Bắc Ninh và Quảng Ninh, cả nước sẽ có 9 thành phố, gồm Hà Nội, Hải Phòng, Huế, Đà Nẵng, TP HCM, Cần Thơ, Đồng Nai, Quảng Ninh, Bắc Ninh. Ninh Bình cũng được định hướng trở thành thành phố vào năm 2030.

title: Indonesia's labor-intensive industries rebound in Q2 2026: Minister
content:
While many countries are losing their industrial sectors, Indonesia is rebuilding its own..Jakarta (ANTARA) - Indonesia's labor-intensive industries are showing signs of a solid recovery, with key manufacturing sub-sectors recording significant growth in the second quarter of 2026, Industry Minister Agus Gumiwang Kartasasmita said.
Speaking at the ANTARA Business Forum 2026 in Jakarta on Wednesday, the minister said that 14 of 15 industrial sub-sectors recorded positive growth, led primarily by labor-intensive segments.
The furniture sub-sector recorded the highest growth at 11.8 percent, followed by footwear and leather at 11.3 percent, food and beverages at 6.5 percent, and textiles and apparel at 6.4 percent.
"These are labor-intensive industries that, about two years ago, were widely reported to be carrying out layoffs. Today, based on our data, these sectors are actually rebounding," Agus said.
He stressed that growth in labor-intensive industries has a multiplier effect on job creation, noting that every percentage point of growth in these sectors absorbs far more workers than growth in capital-intensive industries.
However, some sub-sectors continue to face headwinds. The rubber, rubber products and plastics sub-sector contracted by 7 percent, while basic metals, paper, and tobacco processing recorded relatively sluggish growth.
Citing World Bank data, Agus noted that Indonesia's manufacturing value added reached US$275.61 billion in 2025, ranking 12th globally and first in Southeast Asia—roughly double Thailand's US$137 billion.
The manufacturing sector's contribution to national gross domestic product (GDP) has also risen steadily over four consecutive years, increasing from 18.34 percent to 19.07 percent in 2025.
"While many countries are losing their industrial sectors, Indonesia is rebuilding its own. This is a major asset," Agus said.
The minister added that the national industrial landscape is supported by a strong domestic market of 287.2 million people, with annual household consumption reaching Rp12,834.8 trillion (approximately US$721.05 billion), accounting for 78.39 percent of national manufactured output.

title: MP says 2023 operation created basis for new reconstruction stage
content:
MP says 2023 operation created basis for new reconstruction stage
- 20 September, 2026
- 12:13
The local anti-terror operation carried out on September 19-20, 2023, was not only a logical continuation of the 44-day Patriotic War but also the result of Azerbaijan's long-term political, diplomatic, economic and military strategy, Azerbaijani MP Nigar Mammadova told Report.
The MP said the process that began with the restoration of most of Azerbaijan's territorial integrity in 2020 was completed with the full restoration of sovereignty in September 2023.
"In fact, stopping the 44-day war in November was a conscious choice by Azerbaijan. As our head of state also said, at that time our Armed Forces were just one step away from Khankandi. Following the agreement reached on November 10, 2020, the activities of Armenia's illegal armed formations in Azerbaijan's Karabakh region created serious security threats in the area. Until the Lachin border checkpoint was established on April 23, 2023, Armenian-made mines were being transported into Azerbaijani territories and plans for various provocations were being drawn up. However, Azerbaijan preferred a peaceful solution and offered various opportunities for the reintegration of Armenian residents living in Karabakh within the framework of the Azerbaijani Constitution and laws," she said.
Mammadova said that despite this, the activities of separatist structures, illegal armament and military provocations continued.
"It is no coincidence that on September 19, the Azerbaijani Defense Ministry once again called on formations of the Armenian armed forces located in Azerbaijan's Karabakh region to lay down their weapons and surrender. It stated that the anti-terror measures would be halted in that case. At the same time, on the instructions of Victorious Commander-in-Chief Ilham Aliyev, civilians and infrastructure facilities were not targeted, and only legitimate military targets were being neutralized," she said.
The member of the Milli Majlis noted that the operation lasted only 23 hours and said that formations of the Armenian armed forces located in the Karabakh region and illegal armed groups laid down their weapons, left their combat positions and military posts, and were fully disarmed.
"As President Ilham Aliyev also stated, as a result of the anti-terror operation, which lasted less than a day, separatism was eradicated, Azerbaijan fully ensured its state sovereignty, and international law prevailed. The restoration of sovereignty created the legal and political basis for the full expansion of a new stage of reconstruction in Karabakh and Eastern Zangazur," Mammadova said.
"Three years ago, the anti-terror operation carried out by the Azerbaijani Army ensured the application of state laws throughout the country. The Azerbaijani flag was raised in Khankandi, Khojaly, Aghdara, Khojavend and other settlements. September 20 was declared State Sovereignty Day of Azerbaijan. As President Ilham Aliyev stressed, the chapter of separatism was closed. There will no longer be a place for separatism in Azerbaijan," the MP concluded.

title: Kansas rancher says 50 wind turbines now supply half his income, help keep ranch in family
content:
A Kansas rancher who once worried that wind turbines might change his land says they ultimately did something even more meaningful: They helped keep his ranch in the family.
Since 2006, the 50 turbines on Peter Ferrell's ranch have supplied about half of his income, helping steady a business where revenue can swing widely from year to year.
Here's what to know
In the Flint Hills, Ferrell, a fourth-generation rancher, did not immediately agree to host a wind power project that would become the largest in Kansas. As Good News Network reported, he had to weigh the same objections many rural landowners still hear: that turbines would scar the landscape, endanger prairie chickens, or bring in money seen as out of step with ranching culture.
Ferrell said the turbines have turned out to be easy neighbors, and the biggest change has been economic rather than ecological. The added income has helped protect the ranch from the boom-and-bust nature of cattle production, while cattle still graze the land, the prairie remains intact, and prairie chickens continue to nest there.
After Greenlight Energy Resources took on the development, the effort became the Elk River Wind Power project, which now powers 60,000 homes. That kind of energy generation can help communities reduce their reliance on dirtier power sources while expanding access to electricity produced without fuel costs that can fluctuate over time.
Ferrell said the decision was rooted as much in stewardship as in economics.
"My family has been here since 1888, and that weighs heavily on my decision to engage in practices that can be carried on generation after generation without depleting the resources," he said in a statement. "Both the grass and the wind will be here for generations."
More background
For landowners, wind projects can provide dependable royalty income without requiring them to give up the primary use of their land.
That is especially important in agriculture, where debt, weather, and commodity prices can make it difficult for farms and ranches to survive across generations. A second income stream can help families cover costs, ease financial pressure, and avoid selling land that has been in the family for decades.
Wind power can strengthen local tax bases, create jobs tied to construction and maintenance, and reduce air pollution from fossil fuel generation — a public health benefit that can be especially meaningful for communities downwind of power plants.
Ferrell said that stability has reshaped what is possible for his family's future.
"I have two grown children and four grandkids, and they love this place," he said. "Because of the wind farm, they'll be able to perpetuate it without financial burden."
What's being done?
Across the country, developers, utilities, and landowners are increasingly embracing "working lands" models that allow clean energy projects to coexist with farming and ranching. Ferrell's ranch is one example: The turbines occupy part of the property, but the cattle operation continues.
This kind of dual use does not require an all-or-nothing decision. Families can continue producing food, preserve open land, and add income that helps pay bills and plan for the next generation.
He has also become someone other ranchers turn to when they are considering the same option.
"After the wind farm was built, my phone rang off the hook," Ferrell said. "Farmers and ranchers asking, 'How'd you do it? Could we get one?'"
Where can I learn more?
Wind power can bolster rural economies without pushing agriculture aside. In places such as Kansas and Iowa, that has meant new income for farms and local communities, while major projects off coastal Virginia show how those benefits can grow on a much larger scale.
• On another Kansas ranch, expenses almost prevented him from keeping the farm at all.
• In Howard County, Iowa, wind development generated nearly $3 million for a small farm community.
• Off the coast of Virginia, Dominion Energy completed a major offshore build with broad economic stakes.

title: Rehabilitation initiative at Rawdat Hawtan
content:
The Ministry of Environment and Climate Change (MoECC)’s Wildlife Development Department has organised a rehabilitation initiative at Rawdat Hawtan in the northern region as part of its ongoing efforts to restore Qatar’s rawdas (meadows), enhance natural vegetation cover, and conserve biodiversity and land ecosystems.
The rehabilitation works included planting 300 seedlings of native wild plants and scattering around 5,000 seeds of wild species suited to the site to increase vegetation density, support the natural regeneration of wild plants, and improve the ecological condition of the place.
Adel Mohamed al-Yafei, head of the department’s Plant Wildlife Section, said that the ministry continues to implement plans and initiatives aimed at rehabilitating Qatar’s rawdas and strengthening their natural vegetation cover.
He noted that planting native species and dispersing their seeds form part of national efforts to conserve land ecosystems and protect biodiversity.
Al-Yafei explained that cultivating local wild plants and spreading their seeds contribute to the natural regeneration of vegetation, improve natural habitats, and enhance ecosystem stability.
He stressed that selecting plant species suited to the characteristics of each site is an important factor in the success and sustainability of rehabilitation programmes.

title: “교사가 먼저 배워야”… 안양문화고, AICE 연수로 AI 융합교육 '선도'
content:
AI 추천 뉴스




“교사가 먼저 배워야”… 안양문화고, AICE 연수로 AI 융합교육 ‘선도’


경기 지역의 대표적인 특성화고로 꼽히는 안양문화고등학교 교사진이 주말을 반납한 채 인공지능(AI) 역량 강화에 나섰다.
안양문화고는 지난 12일과 19일 두 차례에 걸쳐 AI 활용 능력 검증시험 AICE(에이스·AI Certificate for Everyone) 연수와 자격시험에 교장·교감·부장교사 등 주요 교원들이 참여했다고 21일 밝혔다. 이번 연수 및 교육은 급변하는 교육·산업 환경에 대응하고 학생들에게 미래 사회에 필요한 역량을 길러주기 위해 교사의 전문성을 높이자는 취지에서 마련됐으며, 교원들은 주말에도 학교에 나와 AI 공부에 매진했다.
시험은 총 6단계다. 비전공자를 대상으로 한 ‘베이식’, 최근 인기가 높은 생성형 AI 활용 능력에 중점을 둔 ‘제너러티브’, 준전공자와 기획자가 대상인 ‘어소시에이트’, 전공자와 개발자 수준에 맞춘 ‘프로페셔널’과 중·고교생 대상의 ‘주니어’, 초등학생 수준에 맞춘 ‘퓨처’가 있다. 이 중 어소시에이트는 2024년 11월 과학기술정보통신부로부터 공인 민간자격을 부여받았으며, 현재 정부 공인 AI 민간자격은 AICE 어소시에이트가 유일하다.
안양문화고가 AICE 자격시험에 주목한 것도 이 때문이다. 단순히 새로운 기술을 사용하는 데 그치지 않고 교원 스스로 AI 역량을 점검하고 전문성을 높여 이를 학생 교육으로 연결하겠다는 목적이다. 이번 연수와 시험은 교사의 AI 역량을 학교 교육에 내재화하기 위한 실천의 하나로 마련됐다.
경기도 안양시 만안구에 위치한 안양문화고는 관광비즈니스과, 엔터테인먼트 비즈니스과, 보건간호과, 웹툰 메이커스과, 금융경영과 등의 학과가 개설된 사립 특성화고다. 안양문화고는 2026년 경기 미래형 직업교육 모델학교로 선정됐다. AI 및 디지털 전환으로 산업현장의 직무가 빠르게 변화하는 가운데, 학교는 AI 기반 지식서비스 실무형 인재 양성을 교육 목표로 삼고 미래 산업에 필요한 직업교육을 강화하고 있다.
교원 대상 AI 연수도 꾸준히 진행 중이다. 생성형 AI 활용 콘텐츠 제작, AI·XR 융합 콘텐츠 프로젝트 지도, AI 수업 내재화 등을 주제로 전문성을 높이고 있다. 특히 이번 AICE 자격시험 응시를 통해 교원들의 AI 역량을 한 단계 더 체계화한다는 계획이다. 교사가 먼저 AI를 배우고 역량을 갖추는 것이 학생의 미래 역량을 키우는 출발점이라는 게 학교 측의 판단이다.
교원의 전문성을 바탕으로 학생들이 AI·디지털 기초역량을 갖추고 프로젝트 학습과 현장실습을 통해 실제 산업현장에서 요구되는 문제 해결력과 협업능력을 기를 수 있도록 교육과정을 발전시킬 예정이다. 지역 기업 및 대학과 협력해 현장 전문가와 대학 교수의 협동수업, 프로젝트 멘토링, 산업체 연계 캡스톤디자인 등을 운영하며 지역과 함께 성장하는 미래형 직업교육 모델 구축에도 속도를 내고 있다.
윤경희 교장은 “AI는 미래 직업교육에서 선택이 아닌 핵심 역량”이라며 “교사가 먼저 배우고 성장해야 학생들에게 변화하는 산업 환경에 필요한 역량을 제대로 길러줄 수 있다”고 말했다. 이어 “앞으로도 AICE와 같은 체계적인 AI 역량 강화 기회를 적극 활용하고 AI·디지털 교육과 산학협력을 더욱 내실화해 미래를 주도하는 AI 융합형 전문인재를 양성하겠다”고 밝혔다.
김정은 기자 likesmile@hankyung.com
안양문화고는 지난 12일과 19일 두 차례에 걸쳐 AI 활용 능력 검증시험 AICE(에이스·AI Certificate for Everyone) 연수와 자격시험에 교장·교감·부장교사 등 주요 교원들이 참여했다고 21일 밝혔다. 이번 연수 및 교육은 급변하는 교육·산업 환경에 대응하고 학생들에게 미래 사회에 필요한 역량을 길러주기 위해 교사의 전문성을 높이자는 취지에서 마련됐으며, 교원들은 주말에도 학교에 나와 AI 공부에 매진했다.
안양문화고 교사들 AICE 자격시험 응시
AICE는 KT와 한국경제신문이 공동 주관하는 AI 능력 검정시험이다. AI 기술의 이해·활용·문제 해결 능력 등을 실습에 중점을 두고 평가한다. 이론 중심의 객관식 시험으로만 치러지는 다른 민간자격시험과 달리 AICE는 응시자가 실제 데이터를 활용한 사례 중심으로 문제를 해결해야 한다.시험은 총 6단계다. 비전공자를 대상으로 한 ‘베이식’, 최근 인기가 높은 생성형 AI 활용 능력에 중점을 둔 ‘제너러티브’, 준전공자와 기획자가 대상인 ‘어소시에이트’, 전공자와 개발자 수준에 맞춘 ‘프로페셔널’과 중·고교생 대상의 ‘주니어’, 초등학생 수준에 맞춘 ‘퓨처’가 있다. 이 중 어소시에이트는 2024년 11월 과학기술정보통신부로부터 공인 민간자격을 부여받았으며, 현재 정부 공인 AI 민간자격은 AICE 어소시에이트가 유일하다.
