title: Development of a phased discharge planning for patients undergoing airway stenting: a Delphi study informed by the timing it right framework
content: ObjectiveThis study aimed to develop a dynamic, phased discharge planning intervention and optimize the nursing care pathway for patients with airway stenosis undergoing airway stenting, to address gaps in complication management and home care competencies following the procedure.MethodsEmploying the Timing It Right (TIR) as a theoretical basis, the initial program was developed through integrated literature review, semi-structured interviews with 7 physicians, 9 nurses and 8 patients, and expert panel group discussions. Subsequent refinement involved three iterative rounds of Delphi consultation with domain experts. Revisions were made based on aggregated feedback to finalize the program.ResultsThree rounds of expert consultation were completed, with questionnaires distributed via email and WeChat. Response rates were 95.24, 100, and 100% across the respective rounds. The expert authority coefficient (Cr) exceeded 0.7 throughout; coefficient of variation ranged from 0.05 to 0.17, 0.06 to 0.23, and 0.06 to 0.19; Kendall’s W values were 0.172, 0.166, and 0.187, respectively (p < 0.001). The final discharge plan comprised 5 primary domains: diagnosis phase (admission to pre-surgery), stabilization phase (postoperative to stable recovery), preparation phase (3 days pre-discharge), implementation phase (post-discharge to 1 month), adaptation phase (1–3 months post-discharge), plus 15 secondary categories and 57 tertiary items. All 57 tertiary indicators satisfied the retention criteria of mean importance score >4.00 and coefficient of variation <0.25 after three rounds of revision.ConclusionThe discharge planning intervention, structured around the Timing It Right Framework, demonstrates scientific rigor and operational feasibility, offering a standardized and comprehensive roadmap for the post-stenting care of patients. Prospective clinical trials are required in future research to quantify its effects on complication incidence, unplanned readmission and patient quality of life.

title: Sensors, Vol. 26, Pages 5924: Fusing Wearable and Environmental Sensors for Context-Aware Firefighter Wellbeing Monitoring
content: Real-time monitoring of on-duty firefighters has the potential to reduce the risk of cardiovascular events and injuries by enabling early detection of fatigue and occupational hazards. Recent work uses wearable sensors to track metrics like heart rate and body temperature. However, most existing systems lack integrated environmental sensing, making it difficult to discern whether elevated vitals stem from physical exertion, ambient heat, or a combination of the two. To address this, a wireless sensing system is proposed that synchronizes physiological and environmental measurements during active firefighting. The system is validated using a new experiment where 28 firefighters completed repeated trials of a training circuit comprising warm-up activities and live-fire suppression. Participants answered survey questions after each phase to gauge overall wellness on a scale from 1 to 10. A predictive framework is developed to classify both the activity type and perceived wellness using the data collected. To extract useful information from the complex multimodal time histories, a series of models are compared using different sets of statistical features extracted from physiological, environmental, and demographic data. Furthermore, a linear mixed-effects (LME) model with subject-specific random intercepts is proposed to account for individual differences in biological response and self-reported wellness. Evaluation demonstrates the system differentiates warm-up from live-fire phases with over 97% accuracy. For wellness prediction, a one-label personalized LME model estimates their later ratings with a mean absolute error of 0.66±0.371, compared with 0.73±0.327 for the same model without personalization. Finally, data investigation reveals that wellness ratings were not fully explained by physiological measurements such as elevated vital signs, with individual differences and demographics accounting for most of the variance. These findings support further evaluation of multimodal sensing and personalized modeling for firefighter monitoring.

title: Replicating the Geometry of Emotion Representations in a Base Open-Weights Model
content: Sofroniew et al. (2026) report that emotion concepts in Claude Sonnet 4.5 are represented as vectors whose geometry mirrors human affect psychology. We replicate the representational core of that study on the base pretrained model google/gemma-2-27b, inheriting every disclosed parameter, resolving unspecified steps by disclosed rules, and changing only the subject model. From 205,200 newly generated Claude Sonnet 4.5 stories matching the original corpus design, we extract 171 emotion vectors and recover the core results. The leading principal components form an affective circumplex (PC1 carries 26.7% of variance against the original study's ~27%, PC2 13.4% against ~14%), emotions cluster into similar intuitive families, and the geometry holds across a broad late-middle band. The valence axis aligns with human norms (r = 0.72, against 0.81) and is stable across scales and depth. Arousal aligns at r = 0.67 (against 0.66) but only at the full 171-emotion scale and late depth, so we do not classify it as replicated. Extending the original analysis, a 46-layer sweep locates a sharp seam at L22-26, where the geometry consolidates and the vocabulary readout becomes legible. An embedding-layer baseline finds much of the geometry already present in the static token embeddings, with arousal as the exception. On top-activating held-out text, the geometry predicts token-level co-activation at r = 0.907. At least 52% of vectors peak on structurally non-conceptual tokens, a measured floor for max-activation confounds. Even when a document contains the vector's emotion word, the peak lands on that word only 6.1% of the time. Because the subject is a base model and the stimuli are Claude-generated fiction, the recovered structure is a property of the pretrained representation of Claude-rendered emotion. The original's causal and assistant-facing analyses are out of scope. Code and data are released.

title: Why Great Plains Ranchers Are Setting Fire to Their Own Land
content:
Smoke hangs thick over southern Oklahoma’s Arbuckle Mountains as flames lick through prairie grass toward a stand of eastern red cedar trees. To many, the scene would look like a disaster in the making. But to father-son ranchers Chuck and Seth Coffey, the fire is a blessing — it’s the best tool for keeping their grasslands healthy and intact.
A growing number of Great Plains landowners, like the Coffeys, are choosing to light their grasslands on fire. Strategic, carefully controlled burns revitalize prairie plants, providing more food for their cattle. Plus, these prescribed burns provide much-needed insurance for managing risk from catastrophic wildfires.
“We burned close to 22,000 acres this year, if you add in all the neighbors,” says Seth Coffey. He’s a fire ecologist and the burn boss on his family’s ranch, the Double C Cattle Company, which spans roughly 30,000 contiguous acres in southern Oklahoma. “When wildfire does happen, we’ve already treated much of the landscape, so we’re dealing with it on our terms.”
The Coffeys and their neighbors burn their land in late winter. By the time strong spring winds arrive that can fan wildfires into conflagrations, no fuel is left to feed the flames.
“If you burn first, the wildfires can’t burn that ground,” says Tanner Swank, grassland biome program manager for Pheasants Forever and Working Lands for Wildlife. Swank helps coordinate prescribed burns across the Great Plains. On several occasions, Swank notes, the Coffeys’ burns have stopped wildfires in their tracks. Even more helpful, local fire departments can then use the already-burned areas on their ranch as a base for beating back the rest of the wildfire.
Prescribed fires are increasingly important in the Great Plains as record-breaking, hard-to-control wildfires continue to make headlines. In March 2025, Oklahoma experienced one of the worst wildfire outbreaks in its history — 30 different fires burned in 44 counties, destroying 300 homes and causing four fatalities. Further north in March 2026, the worst wildfire in Nebraska’s history scorched nearly a half million acres, contributing to the state’s record-breaking fire season.
One reason for these larger, hotter wildfires? The proliferation of woody brush on historically tree-free grasslands.
Past fire suppression efforts allowed trees like eastern red cedar to take over hundreds of thousands of acres of America’s grasslands. Regular burns, lit by Indigenous peoples or lightning, historically kept native trees and shrubs relegated to wet places, like streamsides, draws or springs. But without regular fire over the past two centuries, red cedar and other shrubs are quickly dominating fertile prairies.
Red cedar trees grow fast, reproduce exponentially and suck precious water from aquifers and streams. Plus, nothing grows beneath them, leaving less food for animals. Dense stands of red cedar also up the ante when seasonal wildfires roll through, as trees burn hotter than grasses.

“Eastern red cedars are taking over so much land every day,” Seth says. “It’s increasing the wildland fire risk across the state, and decreasing the amount of forage for livestock and the amount of water available to cities.”
Seth’s father, Chuck, sees the spread of red cedar as an economic drain on ranchers’ income. “It’s your plants that support everything, including the animals,” Chuck says. “Grass comes first, cows second.”
Chuck has made it his lifelong mission to restore native bunchgrasses and wildflowers on his Oklahoma rangelands. “My primary goal is to see every cedar tree die before I go.”
When the Coffeys inherited a portion of their ranch in 2010, the tree canopy cover was 60 percent in many areas. They used prescribed fire, combined with cutting trees and spraying seedlings with herbicides. The hard work paid off — today, tree cover on that part of the ranch is just 17 percent.
“Give it another 10 years, and we won’t have a single cedar tree on the property,” Chuck notes proudly.
The Coffeys quickly learned that prescribed burns work best if they happen across fence lines — and that many hands make light work. They helped start the Arbuckle Rangeland Restoration Association so that ranchers can share resources and coordinate burns at a larger scale. Both Seth and his brother, Aaron, are officers.
Locally led burn associations are “a huge help” for landowners looking to cooperate to maintain productive grasslands, says Swank. He’s seen more and more burn groups pop up across the Great Plains.
“We burn as neighbors,” says Barb Cooksley, a fourth-generation rancher who runs cattle in the Nebraska Sandhills. “We’re all looking for a solution to the same problem.”
The Sandhills region is the most intact temperate grassland left on earth — but encroaching red cedar trees are threatening this unique ecosystem, as well as ranchers’ profitability. “Woody species are increasing year by year. We see more and more of it,” Cooksley says.
Prescribed fire is catching on as a management tool for Nebraska ranchers, though landowners in the Sandhills burn more sparingly than those who live in wetter parts of the Great Plains.
“It’s beach sand. If you bare that with a burn, it responds differently than a heavier soil. It can blow,” Cooksley says. “But we’ve learned that since the Sandhills developed under fire, it’s one of the tools we can use to promote the grass we do have.”
Grassland wildlife, such as birds or pronghorn, are adapted to live in wide-open prairies. These animals suffer as trees close in. “Sharp-tailed grouse and prairie chickens don’t like to nest where there’s trees,” Cooksley says. “Once you remove the woody species, then they’ll come back and nest.”
Fire departments are often “huge fans” of ranchers’ burns, says Seth Coffey. “Ag producers are typically burning problem areas that have a significant wildland fuel risk.”
Prescribed fires are designed to be predictable and controllable — the opposite of most wildfires. Each burn is carefully planned out, approved by the local fire department, staffed with plenty of trained volunteers and professionals, and executed only when conditions are deemed safe. Experienced burn bosses like Seth Coffey direct people and equipment so flames don’t spread beyond the approved boundaries.
“We see continued interest in the formation of prescribed burn associations, which is just exceptional. Ranchers see the point and they see the value of burning,” says Dean Krehbiel, assistant state conservationist for the USDA Natural Resources Conservation Service in Kansas. This agency provides financial assistance to local fire associations to support firefighting training or equipment.
Perhaps the best-known example of landowners regularly setting fire to their pastures is in the Flint Hills of Kansas. Here, in one of the last strongholds of tallgrass prairie in the world, ranchers have been burning for well over a century.
“Historical manuscripts that date back to the 1800s talk about how landowners wanted that landscape burned because they knew their cattle grew better,” Krehbiel says. Fresh new grass post-burn provides more nutrition for livestock.
Satellite technology is also helping ranchers make decisions about where to burn grasslands threatened by encroaching red cedar, Krehbiel says. He points to a free online mapping tool called the Rangeland Analysis Platform, which allows landowners to easily monitor changes in their forage production or see outcomes from prescribed burns.
In any given year, ranchers burn about 2.5 million acres in the Flint Hills alone.
“We light everything on fire,” says Daniel Mushrush, a rancher whose family has been in the Flint Hills for seven generations.
“We all understand that fire is absolutely a needed thing for the tallgrass prairie: the ranchers, the people living in town, law enforcement,” Mushrush says. “This is stuff you talk about at your local bar or when you gather after church. After somebody’s done a burn, we ask, ‘How did it go?’ It’s about as popular as ‘How did the home game go?’ It’s just part of the culture.”
The Flint Hills’ widespread acceptance of fire is still the exception rather than the rule. But prescribed fire’s fan base is growing quickly as more Great Plains landowners learn about the benefits of burning.
“Grasslands are going to burn — it can be on our terms or on Mother Nature’s terms,” Mushrush notes. “That’s really the key: we wait until we can work with the conditions, not against them.”

title: Effect of modernized collaborative care for depression on individual depressive symptoms: A secondary analysis of the eIMPACT trial.
content: Depression affects over 400 million adults worldwide and is associated with substantial morbidity and mortality. Although symptoms vary in their responsiveness to treatment, clinical trials typically report total scores, obscuring symptom-level effects. Despite collaborative care's effectiveness for depression in primary care, its impact on individual depressive symptoms among racially and socioeconomically diverse patients remains unclear. We conducted a secondary analysis of the eIMPACT trial of 216 primary care patients (Mage = 59 years; 78% women; 50% Black; 46% with income <$10,000/year). Participants were randomized to 12 months of modernized collaborative care (internet cognitive-behavioral therapy [CBT], telephonic CBT, and/or select antidepressants) or usual primary care. Two path analytic models estimated simultaneous item-level effects on the Hopkins Symptom Checklist-20 (SCL-20) and Patient Health Questionnaire-9 (PHQ-9). The intervention outperformed usual care on 15 of 20 SCL-20 items and 7 of 9 PHQ-9 items. Seventeen symptoms - including hopelessness, anxious distress, depressed mood, self-blame, worthlessness, disturbed sleep, and fatigue - showed moderate-to-large between-group improvement (βs = -0.50 to -0.70). Smaller but significant gains were observed for six other symptoms (βs = -0.35 to -0.49). No significant advantage emerged for suicidality, loneliness, sexual dysfunction, appetite change, or psychomotor symptoms (βs = -0.03 to -0.37). Modernized collaborative care improves most depressive symptoms in diverse primary care patients, though cross-measure persistent symptoms highlight clinically consequential domains that may be obscured by total scores. Symptom-level analyses may help identify persistent symptom domains requiring targeted adjunctive treatment to optimize recovery.

title: Tanah rizab Melayu Selangor meningkat 1084.55 hektar sejak 2018
content:
Peningkatan itu menjadikan jumlah keseluruhan keluasan Tanah Rizab Melayu di negeri itu meningkat daripada 162,161.98 hektar (400,711 ekar) kepada 163,246.54 hektar (403,391 ekar) di bawah pentadbirannya.
Beliau berkata demikian dalam kenyataan ketika mengulas persoalan yang ditimbulkan berhubung status Tanah Rizab Melayu di Sabak Bernam.
Amirudin berkata tanah seluas 22.41 hektar (55.401 ekar) di Tanjong Karang, Sabak Bernam yang diwartakan keluar menerusi warta yang disiarkan pada 3 Sept 2026 adalah bagi pembangunan Kawasan Pembangunan Sabak Bernam (Sabda).
Bagi mencapai keseimbangan antara pembangunan tempatan dengan kepentingan Tanah Rizab Melayu, tanah seluas 22.41 hektar di Hulu Selangor turut melalui proses pewartaan sebagai Tanah Rizab Melayu.
Amirudin berkata Sabda merupakan usaha kerajaan Selangor untuk membangunkan kawasan anjung utara negeri bagi meningkatkan keterjaminan makanan, selain memanfaatkan potensi agro-pelancongan di pesisir pantai barat Selangor.
“Di samping itu, ia sekali gus meningkatkan peluang pekerjaan bagi warga tempatan,” katanya.
Amirudin berkata usaha itu diterajui anak syarikat kerajaan negeri, Menteri Besar Selangor (Pemerbadanan), dan turut melibatkan komuniti tempatan seperti nelayan, usahawan serta pihak akademia.

title: Intradermal hepatitis B vaccination with or without Imiquimod in cirrhosis after prior vaccine nonresponse: A Randomised Trial.
content: Patients with cirrhosis show impaired immune responses to standard intramuscular (IM) hepatitis B virus (HBV) vaccination, resulting in low seroconversion rates. Intradermal (ID) vaccination and topical imiquimod have been proposed as strategies to enhance vaccine immunogenicity. We conducted a randomized controlled pilot trial to compare three HBV revaccination strategies in patients with advanced chronic liver disease (ACLD) who previously failed standard IM vaccination: IM revaccination, ID revaccination, and ID revaccination combined with imiquimod (ID+IMQ). The primary endpoint was seroconversion at Month 7, defined as anti-HBs titres ≥10 mIU/mL. This monocentric, prospective study included 59 patients with ACLD and anti-HBs titres <10 mIU/mL after prior HBV vaccination. Patients were randomized (1:1:1) to receive either IM vaccination (n=19; Engerix-B® 20 μg IM at Months 0, 1 and 6), ID vaccination (n=19; two 10 μg ID injections at the same time points), or ID vaccination preceded by topical imiquimod 5% application (n=21). In the intention-to-treat analysis, seroprotection rates at month 7 were 36.8% in the IM group, 84.2% in the ID group, and 66.7% in the ID+IMQ group (p<0.01). After Bonferroni correction, only the ID versus IM comparison remained statistically significant (p=0.003). Geometric mean anti-HBs titres were significantly higher in the ID (116 mIU/mL) and ID+IMQ (107 mIU/mL) groups compared with the IM group (12 mIU/mL) (p=0.004). No severe vaccine-related adverse reactions were observed. Intradermal HBV revaccination significantly improves seroconversion in non-responder patients with ACLD compared with IM vaccination, without additional benefit from imiquimod. These results support further evaluation of intradermal vaccination without imiquimod in a phase 3 trial. The study protocol has been registered before the patients' recruitment, in the European Clinical Trials Database (EudraCT) of the European Medicine Agency (2021-000644-22), as well as on ClinicalTrials. gov (NCT05028322).

title: Rwf70bn irrigation project launched in Gisagara
content: The Minister of Agriculture and Animal Resources, Telesphore Ndabamenye on Wednesday, September 23, launched Giseke Agricultural Irrigation Project, with an estimated investment of $47 million (about Rwf70 billion) in Gisagara District. The project, supported by the Chinese government, will develop a 6.5 million cubic metre dam to irrigate about 3,000 hectares through about 48.8km of lined canals. The infrastructure will improve farmers’ access to reliable water, reduce dependence on rainfall and contribute to increased productivity and food security. ALSO READ: Over Rwf330 bn needed to expand Muvumba irrigation scheme The project is also expected to improve farmers’ incomes, create employment, strengthen agricultural value chains and expand market access, supporting more predictable and commercially oriented production. The groundbreaking ceremony was also attended by China's Ambassador to Rwanda Gao Wenqi, development partners, local authorities and farmers. Minister Ndabamenye called on farmers and cooperatives to actively participate in the management and sustainable use of the infrastructure, with a focus on efficient water use, protection of facilities and modern, market-oriented farming. ALSO READ: Major multipurpose dams set to ease water shortages by 2030 Gao highlighted the project as a tangible outcome of China-Rwanda practical cooperation and South-South cooperation, aligned with Rwanda’s agricultural modernisation priorities. Irrigation potential The government's target is to increase the irrigated area to reach 132,961 hectares across the country by 2029, effectively doubling irrigated land within six years. This would raise the share of irrigated land to 27 per cent of total irrigable land, from the current 15 per cent. ALSO READ: Inside Kayonza's irrigation bid to mitigate climate change impacts Currently, irrigation has been developed on 37,273 hectares of marshlands (30 per cent), 10,159 hectares of hillsides (4 per cent) and 27,791 hectares under SSIT (31 per cent). In total, 610,595 hectares of potentially irrigable land were mapped at national, catchment and district levels. More than 417,000 hectares of land with irrigation potential are yet to be developed, a gap the government says must be addressed to boost food security and climate resilience. The potentially irrigable land includes 123,164 hectares of marshlands, 280,351 hectares on hillsides and 89,535 hectares suitable for small-scale irrigation technologies. Rwanda needs at least 693.7 million cubic metres of water storage by 2034 to meet projected irrigation demand.

title: Michigan university installs state's first 'Beaver Deceiver' to stop flooding, spare the beavers
content:
Oakland University is taking an unusual approach to flood control to protect a campus trail without displacing beavers with Michigan's first "Beaver Deceiver."
Here's what to know
After a pair of beavers moved into Galloway Creek in 2023 and built a dam beneath a footbridge, flooding developed along a campus trail, according to USA Today.
On August 12, to manage flooding without removing wildlife, the university installed the state's premier "Beaver Deceiver," or pond levelers—a device that lets water move past a beaver dam without disturbing the animals.
Instead of allowing the stream to back up and spill over its banks, the setup uses a tube resting in the water on both sides of the dam to carry water through the structure. Metal cages protect both ends of the tube, helping prevent beavers from chewing it and making the sound of rushing water harder for them to detect. Because beavers are instinctively driven to block the sound of flowing water, keeping that noise farther from the dam is key to making the device work.
The Clinton River Watershed Council's news release said, "The beavers are not bothered by the device and are free to continue making dams without causing problems for their human neighbors."
More background
Centuries of trapping and trading nearly wiped out beavers, and industrialization and habitat loss have further reduced their range across Michigan. Oakland University also said that Michigan lawmakers gradually came to favor free-flowing streams, leading to policies that encouraged lethal beaver removal.
What's being done?
USA Today reported that Oakland University worked on the project with multiple state agencies, and that the installation was completed under a permit from the Michigan Department of Environment, Great Lakes, and Energy.
While beaver ponds can draw a wide range of wildlife, they can also cause trouble for human infrastructure if water levels get too high.
Project Beaver, an Oregon-based nonprofit, said those ponds can sometimes be "too much of a good thing."
"Similar to the overflow drain in your bathtub, a pond leveler hides the leak in the middle of the beaver pond where they don't think to look for it, while capping the water level at an acceptable maximum height that does not damage human infrastructure," Project Beaver said.
Where can I learn more?
Oakland University's pond leveler works with beavers instead of against them. In other places, beavers are reshaping wetlands, lowering flood risk, and creating habitat — even as nearby communities adjust to the changes their dams can bring.
• In Devon, reintroduced beavers transformed wetlands and helped buffer both floods and drought.
• In west London, beavers built a wetland near McDonald's and helped hold back floods.
• In Scotland, beaver dams trapped pollution as communities searched for sustainable water solutions.
• Across rewilding networks, beaver bombing revived ecosystems where waterways had long been degraded.
• Researchers found beavers boosted bat habitat, underscoring the species' broader ecological value.
Oakland University's project fits into a growing effort to protect infrastructure without giving up the ecological benefits beavers provide.

title: Private Enterprises Step Up to Support Villa Clara Hospitals with Backup Power for Anesthesia Machines
content:
In a significant move, several private enterprises in Villa Clara have donated backup electrical systems to local hospitals. This initiative aims to bolster the operation of anesthesia machines, ensuring the welfare of critically ill patients amidst potential generator failures due to prolonged operation hours.
Official journalist Henry Omar Pérez shared on Facebook this Friday that the delivery followed a call to action by the Communist Party of Cuba (PCC) and the provincial government, coordinated by the UNURE.
As Pérez explained, these private enterprises provided EcoFlow devices to "support the anesthesia machines for critically ill patients in the intensive care units of provincial hospitals."
Pérez noted that while fuel for the generators is currently secured, a pressing concern remains: "Their technical condition could deteriorate due to excessive operational hours."
This acknowledgment highlights that the private sector's contributions are more than mere symbolic gestures; they offer essential security for medical equipment should the generators, crucial for maintaining services during blackouts, fail.
Community Reactions and Official Discourse
The journalist portrayed the donation, with the typical official romanticism, as a demonstration of the "sensitivity" of these private enterprises, publicly expressing gratitude for their assistance. However, the ensuing online discussion offered a different perspective.
One user remarked that donating such equipment was "the least they could do."
Pérez promptly defended the private businesses: "Who told you they are obligated to give anything? They do it out of goodwill, and you respond with a venomous comment," he retorted, adopting a confrontational tone akin to the regime's usual rhetoric on social media rather than engaging in a respectful exchange.
He further challenged: "The important thing is to know what your attitude would be if you had the money and capability. Would you contribute? My question is, what do you contribute, what do you do?"
The Role of Private Enterprises in the Healthcare System
This defense underscores a critical point: private enterprises are not required to provide resources to the state-run healthcare system.
It is these private businesses that are allocating their funds to strengthen vital hospital equipment, which relies on an electricity infrastructure severely strained by the ongoing energy crisis.
Moreover, this situation brings to light a stark reality: the Cuban state cannot independently secure the necessary backup power to protect essential equipment in its hospitals.
The reality, as evidenced in practice, confirms this truth.
Earlier in February, the Ministry of Public Health itself announced a contingency plan in response to energy challenges, which included reducing elective surgical activities and prioritizing urgent and emergency operations.
Months later, official sources admitted that over 100,000 surgical procedures were delayed in Cuba, a statistic that drew sharp criticism after state media attributed these delays to the impact of U.S. sanctions.
Electrical issues have also directly affected critical areas. In April, a blackout in the Intensive and Intermediate Care Units at the Saturnino Lora Provincial Hospital in Santiago de Cuba forced the evacuation of 12 patients, as confirmed by the hospital's management.
Questions about Villa Clara Hospital Support
Why are private enterprises donating to Villa Clara hospitals?
Private enterprises are donating backup electrical systems to support the operation of anesthesia machines in hospitals. This is crucial to maintain patient care during potential generator failures due to prolonged use.
What challenges do hospitals in Cuba face regarding power supply?
Cuban hospitals face significant challenges with power supply due to an overstrained electrical infrastructure and an ongoing energy crisis, leading to potential generator failures and the need for backup solutions.
How has the Cuban government responded to the energy crisis in healthcare?
The Cuban government announced a contingency plan to address energy challenges, prioritizing urgent and emergency surgeries while reducing elective surgical activities.

title: A Living Benchmark for Information Retrieval from Electronic Health Records
content: Large language model (LLM)-based clinical assistants are increasingly being integrated into electronic health record (EHR) systems, transforming how clinicians retrieve and synthesize information from patient records. Their safety and utility depend on rigorous evaluation, yet existing benchmarks are manually curated, costly to update, and rapidly become obsolete with evolving technological advancements. We present a scalable framework that automatically generates question--answer pairs from longitudinal EHR notes. Nineteen clinicians validate the benchmark generator, producing the Benchmark for Retrieving Information in EHRs (BRIE), a continuously maintainable evaluation dataset. Across nine LLMs and five inference strategies, state-of-the-art systems frequently omit clinically important information, particularly for questions requiring synthesis across multiple documents and encounters. Because the generator itself is validated, BRIE supports evaluations that static benchmarks cannot, including the generation of multiple answers that reflect variation in clinician reasoning for robust performance assessment and continuously refreshing benchmark content to guard against leakage. Our results demonstrate that scalable benchmark generation enables rigorous, up-to-date evaluation of clinical LLMs as they are deployed in rapidly evolving healthcare settings.

title: LabourCrew: A Multi-Agent RAG Framework for Trustworthy Adversarial Deliberation and Statutory Reasoning over Labour Law
content: In statutory question answering, every claim must be traceable to evidence, not merely relevant, since unverifiable labour-rights answers carry serious legal consequences. Current systems fall short: single-pass RAG cannot detect insufficient evidence, while multi-agent legal-debate systems treat grounding as a prompting convention, letting agents cite unretrieved evidence. To address this gap, we introduce LabourCrew, a multi-agent RAG framework built around three grounding mechanisms: StatuteGraph, a graph index that explicitly links chapter, section, proviso, and cross-reference structure rather than fixed-length spans; an Evidence Exchange Protocol that confines advocates and an interpreter to an evidence ledger, making citation to unretrieved text impossible, while a fault-tolerant supervisor board runs advocates in parallel so individual failures degrade rather than crash the system; and a Calibrated Trust Gate that replaces categorical accept/reject decisions with a trust score, thresholded via conformal risk control for a distribution-free bound on the false-accept rate. We evaluate on LabourActQA, a 500-item Bangla question set from the Bangladesh Labour Act, 2006, spanning seven reasoning categories and three difficulty tiers. The framework drives the empirical false-accept rate to 0.081, within the target level ($\alpha = 0.10$), achieves the highest Answer Relevancy among HyDE RAG, Graph-RAG, and Hierarchical RAG (0.862 $>$ 0.839, 0.815, 0.828), and degrades gradually rather than catastrophically as question difficulty increases. These results show that calibrated abstention, not retrieval quality alone, is what makes legal question answering auditable in low-resource statutory domains.

title: Governo reforça resposta ao calor extremo com programa que torna cidades mais verdes
content:
O Governo aprovou o Programa de Ação para a Resiliência e Restauro da Natureza em Áreas Urbanas (PRO NAT.URBE), com a publicação em Diário da República do despacho que estabelece a estratégia nacional até 2035 para aumentar a presença da natureza nas cidades e vilas e reforçar a proteção das populações perante os efeitos das alterações climáticas.
A versão final do programa, depois da consulta pública lançada em abril, reforça a componente de execução no terreno. Estão já em curso cinco projetos-piloto, de norte a sul do país, em Évora, Beja, Vila Real, Guimarães e São João da Madeira.
Estas intervenções destinam-se a demonstrar, em contexto real, os benefícios das soluções baseadas na natureza e a criar modelos que possam ser posteriormente replicados por outros municípios. O PRO NAT.URBE prevê projetos de aumento do coberto arbóreo e dos espaços verdes, recuperação de linhas de água, criação de corredores ecológicos, desimpermeabilização dos solos e desenvolvimento de infraestruturas verdes e azuis.
Outra das novidades é a aposta na estruturação de redes de abrigos climáticos em meio urbano, com espaços acessíveis à população durante episódios de calor extremo. Estas redes podem incluir parques e jardins, zonas arborizadas, praças sombreadas e equipamentos públicos, com particular importância na proteção das populações mais vulneráveis.
Para o Ministro da Economia e da Coesão Territorial, Castro Almeida, “é necessário preparar o país para as alterações climáticas que têm particular impacto no nosso território, como bem pudemos verificar com o comboio de tempestades que afetou de forma violenta a região centro, no início deste ano”.
“As ondas de calor são também cada vez mais frequentes e temos de avançar com medidas para proteger a população. Estamos muito empenhados em mobilizar recursos europeus para restaurar espaços verdes em áreas urbanas”, refere Castro Almeida.
“Estamos a passar do planeamento à intervenção concreta no território. Temos cinco projetos-piloto já em curso e vamos avançar com novas intervenções, para demonstrar que mais árvores, mais espaços verdes, linhas de água recuperadas e solos mais permeáveis tornam as nossas cidades mais preparadas para as ondas de calor e para a precipitação intensa. Queremos testar estas soluções, avaliar os resultados e criar modelos que possam ser replicados em todo o país”, afirma a Ministra do Ambiente e Energia, Maria da Graça Carvalho.
O programa responde também às obrigações do Regulamento Europeu do Restauro da Natureza, que estabelece que, até 2030, não exista perda líquida de espaço verde urbano nem de coberto arbóreo urbano, e incentiva os municípios a incorporar estes objetivos nos instrumentos de gestão territorial, nas estratégias de adaptação às alterações climáticas e no planeamento urbano.
O PRO NAT.URBE passa ainda a constituir um referencial estratégico para a programação e mobilização de financiamento nacional e europeu destinado ao restauro da natureza em áreas urbanas, nomeadamente no âmbito do próximo Quadro Financeiro Plurianual da União Europeia.
As intervenções realizadas serão georreferenciadas e disponibilizadas através do Portal da Informação Territorial, o que permitirá acompanhar a execução do PRO NAT.URBE, partilhar conhecimento e disseminar boas práticas entre os municípios.

title: La población del lince ibérico se duplica en 4 años pero 212 murieron por atropello en 2025
content:
La población del lince ibérico se duplica en 4 años pero 212 murieron por atropello en 2025
Biodiversidad
El número de individuos se ha multplicado por casi 30 en 24 años, con una tasa media anual el 24% en promedio
En 2025 se detectaron 273 muertes de lince, de las que 212 (77,9%) fueron por atropello en infraestructuras viarias.
La población de lince ibérico (Lynx pardinus) alcanzó un nuevo registro máximo en 2025. Son ya 2.663 los individuos censados. Esta cifra supone un incremento del 10,9 % respecto al año anterior.
La expansión territorial de la especie, con un total de 18 poblaciones entre España y Portugal, afianza el éxito mundial de conservación de esta especie, que ha logrado prácticamente duplicar el número de linces en solo cuatro años.
Ahora el reto para asegurar la supervivencia de la especie es ampliar su territorio a través de la creación de nuevas poblaciones y acercarla así al objetivo de 3.500 ejemplares y 750 hembras reproductoras, que marca el umbral para salir de peligro, según la valoración de WWF.
Los datos muestran la consolidación de una tendencia demográfica positiva de la especie en los últimos 25 años, período en el que se han desarrollado los programas coordinados de conservación del lince ibérico en España y Portugal.
La población se ha multiplicado por 28, si se tiene en cuenta que el número de ejemplares era de tan solo 94 en el año 2002 (y ahora 2.663). Así lo indica el nuevo censo elaborado por el Ministerio para la Transición Ecológica.
Del total de 2.663 linces censados, 2.269 lo fueron en España (85 %) y 394 en Portugal. Seis han sido las comunidades autónomas españolas que albergaron linces en sus territorios y aportaron datos al censo.
Castilla-La Mancha acogió 1.051 ejemplares (lo que supone el 46,3 % de la población española), mientras que en Andalucía se registraron 885 linces (39 %).
No obstante, en 2025 se detectaron 273 muertes de lince, de las que 212 (77,9%) fueron por atropello en infraestructuras viarias.
Crear nuevas poblaciones es clave
“Si observamos la evolución de los datos de los últimos años, podemos afirmar que las poblaciones más asentadas han alcanzado su capacidad de carga máxima y, por tanto, la estrategia de crear nuevas poblaciones es clave para aumentar el número de linces y que la especie salga de peligro”. señala Ramón Pérez de Ayala, experto en lince ibérico de WWF España
“Por ello, la implicación social y el apoyo de las administraciones públicas de las distintas comunidades autónomas es vital para llevar a cabo nuevos proyectos de reintroducción que aseguren el futuro del lince ibérico”, señala este experto.
Principales áreas de implantación
Las tres principales áreas geográficas para el lince ibérico se encuentran en Sierra Morena, con un total de 1.145 individuos contabilizados.
Este número se reparte por las comunidades autónomas de Andalucía (613 ejemplares en los núcleos de Sierra Morena Oriental en Jaén y Córdoba, y 61 en áreas de conexión de Sierra Morena) y en Castilla-La Mancha (471 linces en varios núcleos de las provincias de Ciudad Real y Albacete). En Extremadura se censaron 302 ejemplares y en la Región de Murcia, 19.
En 2025 se registraron también linces en Castilla y León (11 individuos) gracias al inicio del proyecto de reintroducción en la comarca del Cerrato palentino, y en la Comunidad de Madrid hubo un ejemplar asentado en el este de la región.
Un dato clave: las hembras resproductoras
Del total censado, 1.711 linces fueron adultos o subadultos que presentaron una distribución de sexos equilibrada (824 machos y 791 hembras que pudieron ser sexadas). El número de hembras reproductoras o territoriales en 2025 ascendió a 542, que son 72 más que en 2024.
Este número de hembras reproductoras se aproxima cada año más a las 750 que se considera como hito demográfico necesario para considerar que el lince se encuentra en un estado de conservación favorable.
El número de cachorros nacidos en 2025 llegó a 952, con una tasa de fecundidad de 1,75 calculada como el número de cachorros nacidos entre el número de hembras territoriales.
Colonización creciente
La población de lince continúa expandiéndose y su presencia se ha constatado hasta en 26 núcleos geográficos distintos, en 18 de los cuales se reprodujo en 2025. La tendencia de la población es positiva: en 24 años, la población ha pasado de 94 ejemplares censados en 2002 a 2.663 en 2025.
La especie dijo un gran saltó en su mejora en 2023, cuando pasó de estar “en peligro” a calificarse como “vulnerablee” en la Lista Roja de Especies Amenazadas de la UICN. Las poblaciones continúan creciendo, aunque a un ritmo más lento. Los datos recogidos en los censos de estos últimos años denotan que de 2018 a 2020 las poblaciones crecieron por encima del 30 % y después, entre 2021 y 2024, la tasa de crecimiento ha rondado el 20 %; sin embargo, en 2025 este porcentaje se ha reducido hasta un 10,9 %.
Un censo cada vez más inabordable
El aumento de su población es tan importante que está resultando cada vez más difícil poder registrar e identificar individualmente a todos los ejemplares presentes en los distintos núcleos, dada la gran cantidad de recursos logísticos y esfuerzo que requiere realizar un censo totalmente preciso y completo. Esto resulta especialmente destacable en las dos comunidades autónomas que acogen una mayor proporción de la población en España (Andalucía y Castilla-La Mancha). Es por ello que las cifras dadas para el censo de 2025 habrían de considerarse como un número mínimo de linces.
Los detalles de este nuevo censo se recogen en el informe elaborado por el grupo de trabajo del lince ibérico, que coordina la Dirección General de Biodiversidad, Bosques y Desertificación del Ministerio para la Transición Ecológica con representantes de las comunidades autónomas españolas y del Instituto de Conservación de la Naturaleza y los Bosques (ICNF) de Portugal.
Un ejemplo mundial de éxito
El crecimiento poblacional del lince ibérico en España y Portugal continúa siendo un ejemplo mundial de éxito de un programa de conservación de especies amenazadas. Gracias a los esfuerzos realizados, tanto por las administraciones públicas competentes como por entidades sectoriales interesadas, propietarios y gestores de fincas privadas y sociedad en general, el lince sigue colonizando nuevas zonas.
De hecho, existe un interés creciente por recuperar su antigua distribución en España y son varias las administraciones autonómicas que desarrollan o plantean la ejecución de nuevos proyectos de reintroducción de la especie.
Un total de 273 muertes, de las cuales casi el 80% fueron por atropello
A pesar de las buenas perspectivas para el lince, aún existen factores de amenaza a los que hacer frente para asegurar el alcance de un favorable estado de conservación. Las tasas de mortalidad no natural registrada aún son preocupantes y en 2025 se detectaron 273 muertes de lince, de las que 212 (77,9%) fueron por atropello en infraestructuras viarias.
Ello pone de manifiesto la importancia de avanzar en los trabajos de aplicación de la estrategia de conservación del lince ibérico en España y Portugal, aprobada en 2024 por la Conferencia Sectorial de Medio Ambiente.
Además, “los trabajos de cría en cautividad y la reintroducción de lince ibérico están resultando esenciales para la recuperación del lince”, señalan los técnicos del ministerio. En 2025 se cumplieron 20 años desde el inicio del programa coordinado ex situ.
La cría en cautividad en los cuatro centros destinado a este fin supone un esfuerzo económico muy importante para las administraciones que vienen sufragando este coste con medios propios.
